1.	What correspondence, if any, was exchanged with the government of Great Britain or other overseas
dominions regarding the Singapore Naval Base and its continuation ?
2.	What position did the government of Canada take on the question?
3.	Will the government lay the papers herein on the Table?
4.	Will a time be set by the government for a discussion by this House of the resolution adopted and laid before the Imperial Conference, 1924? If so, when?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1.	The government of Canada has had no communication with any of the other overseas dominions on this subject, excepting such communications as took place at the Imperial Conference. This matter was discussed at the Imperial Conference, and such reference as it was thought advisable to make thereto is contained in the report of the Imperial Conference at page 17. The pertinent paragraph is the following. After quoting certain principles in accordance with which defence should be carried out, section 4 reads:
In the application of these principles to the several parts of the Empire concerned the conference takes note of:-
(a) The deep interest of the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, and India, in the provision of a naval base at Singapore, as essential for ensuring the mobility necessary to provide for the security of the territories and trade of the Empire in eastern waters.
Such correspondence as has taken place with the British government since the conference has related to the form in which an announcement on this subject should be made in the British parliament. I do not think it would be in the public interest to place that correspondence on the Table. There is nothing really confidential about it, but it is, I think, of such a character that the British government would not wish to have it made public at this time. I have, however, in my hand copies of the correspondence, and I propose to pass them over to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), who might look them over and show them to any of the members of his following who may wish to see them. I would ask also that they be shown, upon a like understanding to the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke).
2.	I think at the moment it is not advisable to say more than is in the report of the proceedings of the Conference but I have no objection to stating the position taken by the government at any time the matter may come up for discussion in the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	No commitments or intimations of the nature suggested were made by the Prime Minister or any member of the government in England. The government's position is set out in the letter of the Hon. G. P. Graham (Minister of Railways and Canals), dated February 7, 1924, of which a copy is tabled herewith.
The letter tabled is as follows:
1	February 7, 1924
Dear Sir:
I am now in a position to write you concerning the representations made to the Canadian ministers at the Ritz Hotel, London, on November 5 last, which were to be further considered on our return to Canada. I would have written sooner, but desired to discuss the matter further with my departmental advisers, and also with my colleagues in council, and, as you are no doubt aware, the return to Canada of the Deputy Minister, Major Bell, was unavoidably delayed until quite recently. The position of the Grand Trunk shareholders is admittedly most difficult and unhappy, and it is not without feelings of sympathy for their unfortunate plight that my colleagues and I have again reviewed the circumstances leading to the acquisition of the property. It is beyond question that such arrangements as were made to effect the transfer were considered by all concerned to be the best solution that could at that time be determined. As things turned out, it would no doubt have been infinitely better for the shareholders had the previous management accepted the original offer of the government of rental in perpetuity based upon the average dividends of the ten-year period preceding 1917. That offer was made at a time when no question had arisen concerning the propriety of certain of the dividends paid during that decade; and made also despite the fact that the Drayton-Acworth commission had publicly reported that there was neglect of the physical property in the interest of dividend declarations. It was made also in . the face of the default of the Grand Trunk's subsidiary in respect of the lease of the Transcontinental railway. That the former Grand Trunk management failed to take advantage of that offer clearly cannot be charged to the Canadian government. It is now very evident also that, the delay of the former management in facing an inevitable situation also was most detrimental to the shareholders. Negotiations were deferred until the Grand Trunk Pacific was plunged into actual, and the Grand Trunk draggqjl into virtual, bankruptcy. This, as it turned out, was the determining factor in the award of the arbitrators-the only difference among the three being Chief Justice Taft's view that the Grand Trunk, if left alone, would eventually have recovered. That view was problematic, was opposed to the ascertained facts, and was based upon the disregarding, by the Canadian government, of the Grand Trunk's unfortunate connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
After declining a proposition which was clear cut and definite, involving no uncertainty, such as arbitration, the management agreed, and the shareholders ratified, an arrangement by which the value, " if any," of the preference and common shares should be arrived at. There was contest over the inclusion of the words " if any " in the agreement because it implied that no value might possibly be found. The management was, therefore, aware that there was question as to whether, under all the circumstances, value might be found. The shareholders assert that the award of
the arbitrators was based upon the situation of the Grand Trunk as of one certain day-the date of the assumption by the government of financial responsibility. As a matter of fact, the award was based upon a survey of affairs of the company and its subsidiaries, covering a long period of time, and of the troubles and difficulties which culminated in the agreement finally reached. It was an agreement containing the following clause:
" Grand Trunk Pacific guarantee and claims,-For the purpose of the valuation provided in this agreement, the obligations of the Grand Trunk as guarantors of any indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, or of the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company, or otherwise, and the claims of the Dominion of Canada, against either of the above-mentioned companies, or against any company forming part of the Grand Trunk Railway System, shall not be treated as extinguished or affected by anything contained in the said Act."
After ratifying such an agreement, the shareholders now contend that it should not be enforced, because its enforcement would-in fact, has-wiped out their equity in the property. Recognizing this, the late chairman made a plea for compassionate consideration. Your committee go further and claim (public advertisement in the Citizen, of Ottawa) that " the question of the value of the equity was not settled, and has not been settled yet." To concede such a contention it would be necessary to disregard in toto the conclusions reached as a result of an extended and costly arbitration, confirmed on appeal on a point of law by the Imperial Privy Council.
On this suggestion of equity, the committee's proposal that the shareholders should be permitted the right to participate in future Grand Trunk earnings is no doubt based. To concede such a claim would be to nullify the arrangement under which the value of the stock was ascertained, and, in so far as it was declared to be worth nothing, vested in the Crown by order-in-council, under clause 13 of the acquisU tion agreement. Since the road was taken over, the Canadian taxpayer has had to provide more than a hunlred millions of new capital. Because ofiphe provision of this capital, with consequent improvement of road and equipment the Grand Trunk to-day, under reorganized and resident management, is not th^ Grand Trunk of yesterday under the former management. It is now in a much stronger position and working in close harmony with, instead of competing against, other railways now comprising the National system. In the future earnings of this rehabilitated railway the former shareholders claim the right to participate. In other words, the Canadian taxpayer must find the means to make the road successful-for the benefit of the former shareholders!
It may be urged that recognition of the former shareholders might well be a charge on the railway and not necessarily on the taxpayer. The present management would quite naturally expect to have some say as to such a proposition. Public opinion in Canada is insisting not only on a reduction of taxation, for much of which railway requirements have been responsible, but is demanding as well the scaling down of interest charges which press so heavily upon the management. The scaling down of interest charges could only be effected by writing off loans and advances made by the government to formerly privately-owned roads. Thus, the government is being urged on the one hand to forego any prospect of future interest, and, on the other, to increase its already heavy burden by the reinstatement of former Grand Trunk shareholders to participating rights in future earnings.

speechtext:
For all copy of memoranda, correspondence, telegrams and other documents exchanged between the government of Canada or any of its members and other governments, corporations or individuals, since the first of January 1922, relating to the St. Lawrence waterway route, and the establishment of dams on the St. Lawrence for the development of certain water-powers.
You will not wonder, Mr. Speaker, if to speak of the St. Lawrence river I make use of the language of its discoverer, of the pioneers who explored it to its very sources, of the heroic toilers who settled on its enchanting banks still inhabited by their descendants. It may not, perhaps, be out of place to remind, at the outset of this debate, those who think that the history of Canada only begun in 1759, or a little later, that Jacques Cartier having sailed from St. Malo in 1535, ascended, on his second voyage, the St. Lawrence river as far as Montreal, and from 1615, the time when Champlain together with Etienne Brule explored the St. Lawrence, the Ottawa river, lake Huron and lake Ontario, up to the time when Pierre de la Verandrye and his sons, after his death, and Legardeur de St. Pierre, from 1731 to 1755, explored the water courses of North America, and penetrated as far as the Rocky mountains, all those routes were discovered and explored by Frenchmen, the glorious ancestors of the people of the province of Quebec.

St. Lawrence Waterway
There is nothing, Sir, to be astonished at, if, besides the material interest and sound policy for Canada to prevent the St. Lawrence river from passing into foreign hands, you find us unflinchingly determined, relying upon our veneration of the past, to resist all attempts which, in our mind, would border upon sacrilege. Therefore I was not astonished when, in the city of Sorel, the new Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) acknowledging the congratulations of his fellow-citizens, declared himself entirely opposed to this undertaking. Uncontrollable circumstances prevented me from being present at that demonstration; however, I take advantage of this present occasion to congratulate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on his promotion to the cabinet, and, to express to him all the admiration that I have for his character, his eloquence and all the reliance that I place in him as a safeguard to the interests of the district of Montreal.
In his speech on the Address, the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) expressed himself in the following manner on the subject:
First, no scheme will be entered into at any time as far as I am concerned, and I think it is the policy of the government, until it is clearly shown that the present level of the St. Lawrence river at all points will never be lowered as a result of the works to be carried out: second, that all rights which any of the provinces may possess will be properly safeguarded.
In view of this statement, Sir, I would have felt inclined to allow my motion to pass without adding any futher remarks; but, the day following the statement, a despatch arrived from the President of the United States notifying us that an American committee had been formed, at the head of which were Mr. Hoover and a number of other prominent persons of the United States, who according to newspapers, were all in favour of the scheme. Having come to the conclusion that this announcement took even Ottawa by surprise, I feel it is most important that all correspondence and telegrams exchanged between the two governments should be placed on the Table of the House] The correspondence already published is to the effect that the commission which will be appointed, will examine the report of the International Waterways Commission of 1921 to find out the practicability of the scheme and its cost. May I be allowed, Sir, to state that this commission is fundamentally wrong, because the Conservative government of that date, as usual, had not failed to ignore the rights of the provinces of Quebec in this commission and replaced the Hon. P. B.
38i
Mignault, who, at present is a justice of the supreme court, by Sir William Hearst, exPrime Minister of Ontario.
Useless to add that the Commission having no one on its board to look after the interests of the province of Quebec, these were unsparingly sacrificed in the report of the commission.
The Prime Minister stated, last Monday that the committee which would be appointed to complete the inquiry of 1921, would take no decision which would not have been previously presented to parliament to be ratified. I am sorry to say that this statement to me, is not sufficient. The present government is worthy of congratulations for its policy of economy, we notice that the estimates have been cut down this year. I state, however, that if the government wish to persevere in that policy, they must not be drawn into an undertaking like that of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. I shall be more explicit, I will state that I do not approve of the proposed inquiry in connection with this scheme at the present moment. We have had some experience on the cost of inquiries. Even the initial cost such as salaries to engineers, experts and the incidental expenses of this inquiry is absolutely unjustifiable during the crisis we are passing through. If, Sir, we do our utmost to convince our electors that they are forced or obliged to retrench, if we are to preach to them selfdenial, if we tell them that the government has not even the necessary money to carry out urgent works, to prevent buildings somewhat old from falling into ruins, the more so must we preach to them that the government to start with is cutting down expenditures on a large scale. I think, Sir, that I am able to prove that this scheme should be set aside immediately and this on many scores.
The first is that the cost is absolutely prohibitive, especially under the present circumstances.
The second is that the scheme is impracticable; it will not give the results expected; it will be an economic failure and a disastrous policy both for Canada and the province of Quebec.
Thirdly, I think, Sir, that it is not in the interest of Canada to undertake such a scheme jointly with the United States.
Finally, if it can be shown to us that the dredging of a deep waterway between lake Ontario and the city of Montreal is, under the present circumstances absolutely necessary and that from the economic point of
St. Lawrence Waterway

view Canada is in a position to undertake such a scheme, I state that we should then, instead of deepening the St. Lawrence, build the Georgian Bay Canal route.
If you will allow me, Sir, I shall briefly pass in review, the various contentions that I have enumerated. I mentioned that the cost was prohibitive, we have not forgotten how this St. Lawrence waterway scheme started.
In 1920, a commission was appointed composed of members of both the United States and Canadian governments. This commission appointed two experts the late Mr. W. A. Bowden, Chief Engineer of the Department of Railways to represent Canada, and Colonel W. P. Wooten, an American expert to represent the United States; a report was made in July, 1921; these experts estimated the cost of the construction of the St. Lawrence canal at $253,000,000. If we add to this amount an additional $18,000,900 that the experts have stated to be necessary to bring the depth to 30 feet, and moreover the cost of the development of the water-powers on the St. Lawrence, which the experts have further estimated to cost $236,000,000 we arrive at the total amount of $507,000,000 and even this amount does not cover all the cost3. A prominent American engineer, Hugh L. Cooper, stated that the cost of deepening the St. Lawrence including the deepening of the canals, the development of the water-powers, would be $1,420,000,000. He further remarked that in winter there would be but 30 per cent of the water powers that could be utilized. But this is not all, so as to make this waterway useful, in order that the deepening of the St. Lawrence may fulfil the aim in view, it is absolutely necessary that the ports on the Great Lakes be deepened in such a way as to allow ships drawing 26 to 30 feet to enter those ports. At present the mean depth of the Great Lakes is 21 feet. In order to obtain a depth of 25 or 30 feet, it would first be necessary to dredge the St. Mary's river, between lake Huron and lake Superior; the St. Clair river between lake Huron and lake St. Clair. The deepening of the Chicago harbour would cost $10,000,000. We find close to the city of Buffalo a mean depth of 10 to 15 feet and it is only three miles out of the harbour of Buffalo that there is a depth of 30 feet which is necessary to make use of this canal. That only goes to show the additional cost of this scheme, it does not include the sum which would be needed for the harbour of Toronto and those of other Canadian cities situated on the Great Lakes to allow free access to ships drawing 25 to 30 
feet of water. This, Sir, will give you an idea as to the cost of this scheme.
I was calling your attention, Sir, to the fact that it would be unreasonable for the government, owing to the economic crisis we are at present passing through, to disburse money for this scheme, I brought to your attention, Sir, the fact that we found it hard to convince the citizens of this country, in our respective constituencies, that even urgent and necessary work could not be carried out because the government had not the means to do so. For my part, Sir, there is a project which affects not only my two counties but the development of the city of Montreal, and I may say the province of Quebec and the whole of Canada, it has been discussed for many years. I refer to the construction of a new bridge between Montreal and the South shofre. Were I to tell you Sir that the means of communication between Montreal and the South shore are actually less than they were in 1890, you would likely be astonished; however such is the case. In 1890, to connect the city of Montreal to the South shore, there existed on the Victoria bridge two vehicle roadways of 13-J feet. There did not exist, at that time, any motor car traffic there was very little tourist traffic. In 1910, one of these roadways was kept for vehicles, the other was given to the Tramway Company, so that the only means of communication for vehicles of all kinds, between the city of Montreal and the South shore, at present, consist in a Roadway of 13j feet in width. The conditions are entirely inadequate to the amount of traffic, they are dangerous and all those who have crossed the Victoria bridge have been able to satisfy themselves as to the danger that exists in crossing this bridge and the inefficiency of the means of communication. I have no desire, Sir, in this speech of requesting the government to vote the necessary funds fo|r the construction of a new bridge, but I am here to protest against the expenditure of fabulous amounts for a scheme of which it is impossible to foresee the results,-such as the St. Lawrence waterway,-before we undertake the useful and necessary expenditure of building a new bridge.
As a general policy, Sir, no government should spend such considerable amount unless it is first assured that this expenditure is in the interest of the country. If I clearly understand the scheme of the promoters,-and I have been receiving pamphlets favourable to the scheme since the beginning of the session,-their aim is to deepen the

St. Lawrence Waterway
St. Lawrence and the canals as far as the Great Lakes so as to allow ocean vessels to reach these lakes. I contend, Sir, that seagoing vessels, will never be able to compete successfully with ships on the Great lakes. This question was considered by the Shipping Federation Board of Canada; it was studied by a number of engineers specially conversant with the subject and the result was found to be as follows: Ocean steamers cost 80 per cent more than lake steamers; the latter have three times the cargo space with the same draught. This is easily explained: On the Great lakes you have very short waves, you are not forced to build ships with the same rigidity, the same strength, consequently you have not to lay out the same amount for construction as for the ocean steamers which are obliged to battle against much longer waves when crossing the ocean.
Now, there is one thing absolutely certain: If the ocean steamers were used to carry the wheat ijrom the West to Montreal, they would be forced to return West without any cargo. It is a well-known economic principle, in the maritime world, that a ship which carries a cargo but one way and is obliged to return without cargo, cannot pay its way.
This is, Sir, in my opinion, one of the strongest reasons to prove the futility of wanting to have ocean vessels reach the Great Lakes.
It was stated that the construction of this waterway would bring down the cost of transportation of wheat. I see the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) in his seat. He introduced, a few days ago, a resolution, in which he contended-he must know of what he is talking-that the cost of transportation on wheat, from the West to Montreal, would not be lowered by the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. Moreover, the transportation by inland navigation, the transportation by rivers or lakes is, at present, an economic failure everywhere. Take for instance, all the canals that exist in America, all have proved a failure, all show, in their reports, at the end of the year, large deficits. The Mississippi canal, called the "Mississippi Warrior" has accumulated a deficit, since 1917, of $2,036,608; the Panama canal, has yearly deficits and the canal known as the "New York State Barge" is in the same predicament. Look at our own waterways, from Niagara to Montreal, if you look into the transportation of freight, from 1908 to 1914, you will find that there has been 8,279,477 tons of freight which were carried during these six years. Now, from 1914 to 1922-and yet we include in these the years of war during
which the freight should have been greater- we find, instead of 8,279,477 the total freight transportation reduced to 5,424,420. The cause is quite simple; the shippers fight shy of the canals, they have misgivings in regard to water transportation, and the quicker they can send their goods to ocean ports the better they like it. We already have accidents with boats of three thousand tons in the canals, when a boat of the above tonnage hits the door of a lock, it means that perhaps, for five or six days or a week, the boat is held up. Wheat shippers are under contract to deliver their merchandise in Europe; all manufacturers of this country who carry on exportation, are under contracts, mostly on fixed dates, their goods must reach their destination within a time limit, now, they do not wish to run the risk of seeing their goods held up in the canal and delayed for five or six days or a week. If these three thousand tonnage boats are the cause of rather numerous accidents in our canals, so much more will it be the case should we be using 15,000, 20,000 or 25,000 ton ships.
Another reason given, it is claimed-I think it is the contention of some of my hon. colleagues of the West-that we shall economize large sums in the cost of the transportation of wheat. Let us suppose that we have a crop of, say, 400,000,000 bushels, and let us agree that we economize three cents per bushel, this would, amount to $12,000,000.
If the cost of this canal system amounted to only $300,000,000-and I think that I have shown that it would cast at least $500,000,000 -we shall have to pay an interest amounting to $15,000,000 per year, plus $2,000,000 for maintenance, this means a total amount of $17,000,000 that we shall disburse to economize $12,000,000. This establishes clearly that the St. Lawrence waterway scheme, economically speaking, admits of an expenditure which is at present unwarranted.
Moreover, I think that we should, by now, be wiser regarding our transactions with Americans. And this brings me to my third point: That it is not ini the interest of Canada to construct so expensive a waterway system jointly with the United States.
In 1921, the International Waterways Commission's report was published, hon. members will recall some of the petitions that were presented to the United States Congress and Senate. Hon. members will recall that Senator King from Utah, introduced a motion to the effect that Canada should cede to the United States the whole territory comprised between the Richelieu river, lake Champlain and the northern boundary of the state of New York, Congressman Ten Eyck introduced a bill in
St. Lawrence Waterway

congress to purchase from Canada the whole territory to the south of the St. Lawrence, all Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. A neutral zone like that of the Panama canal* was proposed. Experience should have made us wise. The result of the war of 1775 which ended by the Treaty of Versailles, in 1783, swept away the whole territory to the south of the Great Lakes, part of Minnesota, all the states of Wisconsin Michigan, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio.
We were despoiled of the iron mines of lake Superior, the copper mines of Michigan, the oil fields of Indiana, Ohio, Illinois, the bituminous coal of Indiana and Ohio, part of the anthracite coal fields of Pennsylvania and finally 300 miles square of the richest territory in the world.
This proves, Sir, the ravenous appetite of our neighbours. We must also bear in mind the treaty of Ashburton and the treaty where we afterwards lost part of Alaska. Each time our best interests were sacrificed to the advantage of the United States.
The political aspect in regard to this project is therefore important. It is stated in the report that the cost would be proportionate to the benefits which the two countries would derive from it. Can you imagine our position in the face of the United States, who would probably be deriving 70 per cent of the benefits of the construction of this waterway having paid 70 per cent of the cost of the work? You can well form an opinion, Sir, regarding the situation of the representatives of Canada on a board of management of which 70 per cent of the members would be United States citizens.
We have still had a more recent test. Years ago the city of Chicago emptied its sewers in the Chicago river. The latter emptied in lake Michigan. It was claimed that, from a sanitary point of view, they would have to divert the waters of the Chicago river. A treaty was concluded, in 1910, between Canada and Washington by which it was agreed to divert the water course of the Chicago river-which emptied until then in lake Michigan-so as to give it an outlet in the Mississippi basin, on the well defined understanding that the total quantity of water which would thus be diverted from the Great Lakes would be 4,160 cubic feet per second, at the most. At present, 10,000 cubic feet of water is being diverted. The Canadian government protested. I am even informed that the Washington government itself protested to the authorities of the city of Chicago. It was of no avail; they continued to divert 10,000 cubic feet, and in one year 
alone the fact of taking 10,000 cubic feet of water has brought down the water level of the St. Lawrence, at Montreal, ten inches, causing $300,000 damages. Do you wish for another example? In 1918, the company known as the St. Lawrence Power Company was incorporated. It requested from the International Waterways Commission their leave to construct a dam at Massena, New York. The Canadian government opposed this request. A counsel representing the Canadian government went to Washington to protest Noticing that their protests had no effect, the government passed an order in council to further protest, in a more official manner. The Massena dam still remains, notwithstanding the protests of Canada. It is nothing more or less, that the United States government adopted in this circumstance a policy of "don't give a hang." It is the same policy which would prevail if we had the misfortune to enter into an agreement with them allowing to the two countries, a joint control on the St. Lawrence river.
There is no necessity, Sir, to mention the danger that would exist for navigation between lake Ontario and Montreal if this waterway scheme was carried out and if, at the same time, dams were constructed for the purpose of the water powers. All those who are interested in navigation, the Shipping Federation and other interested companies, are all unanimous in saying that these dams would lower the level of the river, at Montreal, and between Montreal and Quebec, and consequently, would prevent between these two ports, the navigation of heavy draught ocean steamers.
I think I have clearly established that the scheme is impracticable owing to its great cost, the results which would follow, and, owing also to the bad policy which would result from admitting the United States to a joint control with us over the St. Lawrence river. However, if, as I mentioned at the outset, it could be shown that it is in the interest of Canada to have a deep waterway between lake Ontario and the port of Montreal, if it could be shown also that the finances of Canada can sustain such an expenditure, I state, that before even thinking of constructing the St. Lawrence waterway, we should build the Georgian Bay canal. We would thus have an all Canadian route, we would have a waterway which would be in Canadian territory from its head waters to its outlet into the Atlantic ocean, a route three hundred miles shorter than that of the St. Lawrence river. By the St. Lawrence route, the distance is nine hundred and forty-three miles between Sault Ste. Marie and Montreal, by the

St. Lawrence Waterway
Georgian Bay canal way, it would only be six hundred and sixty one miles. We have reports of well known engineers on this scheme.' I shall only mention one, Mr. Arthur Surveyer, president of the Institute of Engineers of Canada who stated that the Georgian Bay canal and the development of the rivers and lakes situated along the water course of this route would supply 1,000,000 horse-power, over and above the 2,500,000 horsepower that could be developed in that part of the St. Lawrence in Canadian territory. I might further add that this route is easier to build owing to the smaller volume of water. The Ottawa river not being as wide as the St. Lawrence river, the dams would not be sc wide, and therefore would be less expensive; there would exist more safety for navigation: we would thereby avoid lake Erie, which is exceedingly dangerous and where shipwrecks are of frequent occurrence, and finally, we would develop Northern Ontario and Quebec; we would open up a mining country which h^s not its equal in the world, and we would be building, as I said a moment ago, a route which would be entirely in Canada, and thereby accomplishing a truly national work.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to add to all these arguments that we must protect our St. Lawrence, that we must safeguard it as a sacred trust bequeathed by our ancestors, and resist with all our strength that it may not become an international river.
The propaganda emanated from the United States. It is not astonishing that they eagerly covet the most important and beautiful asset of our country. Cartier had alreadly noticed this lust when he wrote, more than fifty years ago, these patriotic verses:
L'etranger voit, avec un ceil d'envie,
Du Saint-Laurent, le majestueux cours,
A son aspect le Canadien s'ecrie:
O Canada, mon pays, mes amours.
If we wish, Sir, that these verses remain true, we will not divest ourselves of any part, even trifling as it may be, of this inheritance. Let us therefore, oppose with all our strength any ambitious attempts of our neighbours, and, politely but firmly tell them in a language they will understand "Hands off the St. Lawrence."

I have no objection to the
motion of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault); in fact, I was thinking of putting on the order paper a similar motion myself in regard to the production of papers, telegrams and correspondence of all kinds on this subject. Another reason why I do not iwish to deal with the question at length is because the government have recently stated through the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that they are about to have a thorough investigation made of the whole question.
I tried to follow my horl. friend in his eloquent French, but I am afraid my French is rather limited, and I could not follow him as well as I should have desired. But I think I caught the drift of most of his arguments. I take it that from the standpoint of the province of Quebec or of the city of Montreal he is strongly opposed to the St. Lawrence waterway project and holds the view that if we do anything of this sort we should devote our attention to the Georgian Bay canal scheme. He also suggested, if I understood him correctly, that a bridge might be built in his constituency which would be of much more importance to the country as a whole than the building of either of these canals. I have no objection to his standing up for his constituency. He always does that, as the rest of us do for ours, and I do not wish to argue against that either. But I understood him to give the opinion of an engineer, Mr. Cooper, of New York, that the cost of this project would be $1,400,000,000.

He presented that figure
in opposition to the estimate of the engineers of the International Joint Commission that the work would cost about $252,000,000.

Will my hon.
friend permit me to correct him? The engineer of the International Joint Commission stated that the cost would be $253,000,000, but this was without the development of the water powers, which would cost $236,000,000, bringing the total estimated cost up to $489,000,000.

My hon. friend is wrong
in that. I do not happen to have any cf the literature at hand, because I did not know that this question was coming up today. But I know that the figure given by the engineers of the International Joint Commission was $252,000,000, and that included the development of all the power in the international section of the river; in fact, it included the development of a million and a half horse-power of electricity. I am positive that if my hon. friend looks up the report he will find that this figure

is correct. I am sorry I have not the report here, but I am quite familiar with the figures because I have read them many times. I well remember a speech by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), on my hon. friend's own side of the House, in which he brought out that very argument.
I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but will he tell the House what he means by the development of power in the "international section" of the river?

There is a part of the
river, between Prescott and Cornwall, I think, although I am not sure I have the exact stations, but there is a part of the river east of Kingston, which is really international, running between the province of Ontario on the north and the state of New York on the south. Below that section you come to the really national part, so far as Canada is concerned, that is where the river runs between the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario or through the province of Quebec.

The $256,000,000
does not include the cost of that second part.
I agree, but it does include the cost of the development of 1,500,000 horse power on the international section.
For the Americans.

No, it is international power, to be divided between the two countries. Canada has as much right to half as the United States has to the other half. The $252,000,000 includes not only canalization but the development of that 1,500,000 horse power on the international section, and the report of the International Joint Commission claims that that 1,500,000 horse power could be developed so cheaply that in all probability the return from the electricity developed would pay the interest and sinking fund on the whole undertaking. My hon. friend shakes his head, and I know there are others as well who do not agree, but I am simply quoting from what the engineers say in the International Joint Commission's report. So the jump from $252,000,000 up to Mr. Cooper's figures is sufficient to cause further investigation, and in that I have no quarrel with the government.
In regard to the Georgian Bay canal, I think no Canadian would object if something was to be gone on with and the country 
could finance it, but personally, as between the two, I think that if we could develop the St. Lawrence route it would be better for the country as a whole because of the lesser expense so far as Canada is concerned, for the United States would pay half the expense. The International Joint Commission not only included that $252,000,000 in the total expenditure, but the $80,000,000 or $90,000,000 which is being spent anyhow by the Canadian government on the Welland canal. So if these figures are correct, Canada's share in developing the St. Lawrence route would be very much less than the cost of building the Georgian Bay canal. I looked up the figures a few months ago, and I remember that away back in 1904 or 1905 the probable cost of the Georgian Bay canal was estimated to be about $100,000,000. Of course, to-day with the higher cost of everything, that would be doubled or trebled. I was going on to say that the Georgian Bay canal from the Canadian standpoint, and certainly from the standpoint of western 'Canada, would be just as advantageous as the development of the St. Lawrence route. But when you consider that the cost of the St. Lawrence route is to be divided, and the fact that there are some 36,000,000 people in the United States who are much more tributary to the St. Lawrence project than they are to the Georgian Bay canal project, it makes the St. Lawrence project much more feasible from the standpoint of bringing about a new route for traffic.

In what states are those
30,000,000 people?

I do not mean in the
states directly bordering on the Great Lakes; but the states of North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota and Kansas, for instance, which do not border on the Great Lakes, are tributary to the Great Lakes inasmuch as their produce, wheat and so forth, is carried over the Great Lakes, and the states that are tributary to the Great Lakes in, that way include about 30,000,000 people, and these same states, it is claimed by the authorities, also produce some seventy per cent of the food and raw materials produced in the United States. I am giving these figures from memory from the International Joint Commission s report, and I am quite sure that my memory serves me correctly in this case.
My hon. friend from Chambly and Ver-.cheres (Mr. Archambault), if I understood him correctly, also took up the question of

St. Lawrence Waterway
ocean boats going up the Great Lakes. I am not one of those who ever had a picture in my mind of ocean boats using these canals, if they are built and proceeding up the lakes to Toronto, Fort William, Chicago, Buffalo and other cities. But what would happen if this project was undertaken would be that the boats carrying wheat from the prairie provinces, instead of stopping as they do to-day at Georgian Bay ports, or at Port Colbome and transshipping to Montreal, or transshipping to New York via Buffalo would continue on to Quebec or Montreal, and one of these two cities would still get the traffic. I do not think there would be any injury to Montreal. And in that connection I would just like to give one thought that I think the people of Montreal and of that district should consider very seriously before making too much opposition to this whole scheme. If you will look at a map of the United States and Canada together you will find that from Oswego at the southeast end of lake Ontario to the Hudson river there is only a very short distance which would require to be canalized to have lake and ocean steamers traverse the Hudson river and out at New York, and the New York people are to-day very strongly advocating-especially in view of the opposition of some Canadian people to the St. Lawrence scheme-the building of a canal system from the Hudson river across to Oswego. If that scheme were gone on with, they claim, it would be cheaper for the United States than paying for their half of the St. Lawrence development, and! Montreal and Quebec would bq to a very large extent sidetracked because much of the traffic which now goes to them and which would certainly go to them by way of the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes system-

Is it not a fact that the
strongest ground the promoters of this scheme are taking is that ocean boats would go right up the lakes? I am not saying that it would be a bad thing, even if it did affect Montreal and Quebec.

Some people take that
stand, but those who have given the subject a great deal of study-and from the layman's standpoint I think I can claim to be one of those-do not take that view, except as regards tramp steamers, but that the boats instead of stopping at the points I mentioned a moment ago would continue to Montreal or Quebec and trans-ship there. It would save trans-shipping at Georgian Bay ports or at Port Colborne. The grain from the West could be transported right through to Montreal, and it would convey to Montreal or Quebec, whichever got the traffic, much of the American traffic which now goes by way of Buffalo, because up to very recently-two or three years ago-about sixty and sometimes seventy per cent of all our Canadian wheat carried from the head of the lakes was taken to Buffalo and trans-shipped by the Erie canal to New York. I repeat in all sincerity that if this St. Lawrence scheme were gone on with Montreal stands to gain in every possible way, and not to lose at all, because she would get not only a large proportion of the Canadian traffic which she does not get now, but a large proportion also of the American traffic which she does not get now to any great extent.
Particularly am I impressed with the point that I mentioned just a few moments ago, that Montreal and the cities in that district should very seriously consider the danger of the American people deciding to build a canal from Oswego to the Hudson river. That project is very strongly supported. I think it was the New York Times, probably the strongest paper in New York, that came out in support of that scheme only recently. Certainly if it were gone on with, it would be a very serious matter for Montreal.

Does my hon.
friend seriously contend that if the St. Lawrence project reduces the depth of the water in the St. Lawrence from Montreal to Quebec, it will aid the development of that district?

I do not admit it would do any such thing. Neither do the engineers. My opinion is of no weight whatever on that question, because I do not pretend to have any engineering knowledge, but very good engineers claim positively that there would be no change in the levels of the waters below the canalization or the power scheme development. However, that is an important question, and if the further investigation which is to be made should show that that would be brought about, then of course there is much more reason perhaps for Montreal to seriously consider the matter.
I should like to touch one other point that my hon. friend (Mr. Archambault) made in regard to the saving concerned in this scheme. He mentioned, if my understanding was correct, that in the operation of this scheme he figured the cost would be something like $300,000,000, laying aside Mr. Cooper's figures, and he took the interest upon that, and figured it to be $15,000,000 and then said that the gross saving would amount to $12,000,000. I think that was his estimate of the saving on the grain of the West.

I thought I understood him. Then let us assume his figures are correct. I will not argue about them, though they are very much lower figures than those given by Mr. Herbert Hoover, who is a member of the American cabinet to-day. Furthermore, the figure of ten cents was given by Mr. Julius Barnes, whom everybody in the House knows. He is one of the best authorities in the world in regard to the handling of grain; and he made the statement that there would be a saving of ten cents a bushel on the wheat from Canada and the United States. It would be not only on the wheat shipped out, because that wheat fixes the price of the wheat left in the country.

What is the actual cost?
Mr. MANION; The average cost last year from Fort William to Montreal was about twelve cents.

You would save
ten cents out of twelve.

No, I did not say that; I simply quoted Mr. Julius Barnes as saying it would save ten cents a bushel.
Let me point out to my hon. friend that once a cargo is put upon a steamer it costs very little more to carry it a long distance than to carry it a great deal shorter distance. You can carry freight to-day, I am informed, from New York to Bombay and from New York to Calcutta at exactly the same price, though the distance is two thousand miles greater for one than for the other. I am giving that as an illustration of the cheapness of carrying freight on boats, though I would not claim that ten cents would be saved out of twelve, I was simply quoting Mr. Barnes' figures. The price the year before-and my hon. friends from the West will bear me out-would not be the average price of twelve cents but nearly double that from the head of the lakes to Montreal.
I was going to point out another saving. In addition to the saving on grain we have the revenue from the horse-power; because the horse-power can be developed, engineers claim, on this section, at a very low cost, and can be sold at a sufficient price to pay not only the interest but also the sinking fund upon the scheme.
Referring to the great objection my hon. friend made with regard to any dealing between the United States and Canada, he appealed to our Canadian nationality, to our great 
patriotic feelings, against uniting with the United States in a deal such as this. Well, I must confess frankly that I have not those feelings in the matter that he seems to have. At the same time I do not wish to be misunderstood, I do not want to be understood as not advocating that we should take every precaution, if this deal were ever proceeded with, to look out for our own interests'. One thing I have always noted with reference to the United States is that when they go into any deal they are very careful to look after their own interests, and I admire them for that. No one knows that better than my .hon. friends to my left, because the United States are looking after their interests to the extent of barring out anything produced in Canada if it suits them to do so. I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Archambault) that all precautions should be taken, but I do not agree that it would be necessary to find this an insuperable obstacle to the progress of the scheme.
I hesitated to speak on this question, but I felt there were a few points that should be laid before the House, and particularly the point which I will take the liberty of emphasizing another time; namely the possibility of the building of a canal system from Hudson river to Oswego, which would certainly do more harm to Montreal than this scheme would do.

In
common with my hon. friend from Fort-William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), I was unable to understand the drift of the discussion on the other side on this question -in fact I was not able to understand any of it. It was not until my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River spoke that I could catch more than the drift of it; and as I spoke very briefly on this question the other day-in fact I did not speak on this phase of it at all-I would like to make some observations on one phase of it, namely the saving on a cargo of grain. I have been trying to arrive at what would be a reasonable saving, and I have approached the question in this manner. The Canadian people at the present time are building the Welland canal, and whether the international project proceeds or not, we are going to have the Welland canal completed in a few years. That project will permit boats to load at Fort William and proceed to the eastern end of lake Ontario. The largest boats will carry their cargo there. The fact that it will be some years before we can complete the St. Lawrence waterway, even if we decide to start

St. Lawrence Waterway
at once, and the fact that we would have the Welland canal completed several years before the St. Lawrence scheme could be completed, mean that it would be necessary to build elevators at the eastern end of lake Ontario. It would be possible, of course, to transfer the wheat by floating elevators into barges; but as we will have to handle grain for even four or five years, I think it is a foregone conclusion that we would have to build some elevators at the eastern end of lake Ontario. According to the figures in other harbours, the cost of transferring grain from cars into boats through an elevator, rendering the same service as we would render at Prescott or Kingston, only in the reverse order-and I take it the cost in this case would be about the same -is a cent and a half a bushel. Hon. members will understand that I am making a comparison between the cost of handling the grain from the eastern end of lake Ontario to Montreal, and the cost as it would probably be after the St. Lawrence was deepened and the large boats were able to proceed to Montreal. If the cost of transferring the grain from the large boats through the elevator to the cars is one and one-half cents, we add to that the railway cost from Prescott, if we take Prescott, which is only 108 miles from Montreal. Taking the average of a long haul, the cost would be only a cent and a quarter. But owing to the fact that it is a short haul, it would only be fair to add considerable to that cent and a quarter, say we call it two cents and a half. Now, we have the grain carried from the boat at the east end of lake Ontario and placed beside the elevator at Montreal for four cents a bushel.
This covers all charges, and that I take it is a very liberal margin, considering that before 1910 in some years the average cost of carrying grain from Fort William to Montreal was only four cents. Now, suppose that we proceed with this project and that we are able to proceed upon the St. Lawrence with large boats to Montreal, there is now and always will be from 30 to 40 miles of canals, depending of course upon what you call a canal; I suppose there are places on the river where there will have to be a little dredging, but it is figured at from thirty to forty miles of canal. In these canals boats cannot move rapidly. In the Panama canal and some other large and differently constructed canals they can move at 5J and 6 miles an hour. But in such a canal as this, engineers put the rate at four knots an hour, even though the vessels may be able to go at twelve or more knots an hour on the open water. The dangers are greater and the insurance will be higher than on the open water. One can readily see that, with a depth of even twenty-five feet, where depth is no impediment, boats cannot proceed down thirty-three miles of canal to Montreal and back again without making a considerable charge. All that will be saved will be the cost of such transportation by large boats from the end of lake Ontario to Montreal as against the route which I have just mapped out by rail. If the higher is only four cents and the lower must be something considerable, where under the heavens, I might say, are .you going to get a saving of ten cents?
Let me set forth another factor in this connection. It is quite possible that the grain may be transferred by floating elevator to barges-these proved very satisfactory at New York-down this canal at a cheaper rate than the railway could carry it. If so, then the saving would be between four cents and the new rate under the better conditions; but it would be between the barge rate and the rate of the large boats after the canal is completed.
Does my hon. friend know the rate from Buffalo to New York via the Erie canal during the season of navigation?

I do not know it exactly,
but I know that about a year ago eighty per cent of the grain that was going into New York went in by rail, not by the Erie canal. There is an argument that, I think, is worth while taking note of. The Erie canal has not been able to compete with the railway, and it is a question in my mind whether a canal that is deeper-that canal is just a large ditch-where vessels can go at only four or five knots an hour will have much advantage over the all-rail route.

As a matter of fact, I
know the rate. The rate is from eight to ten cents on the Erie canal. As my hon. friend says, it is much in the shape of a ditch; it does not amount to anything; it is only for a few flat boats. The reason I asked the question was this. The same conditions, more or less, exist to-day east of Port Colborne, from Port Colborne to Montreal, as my hon. friend knows. He quoted a figure of four cents, but he did not give me the dates. I know he showed me the figures at one time, and about fifteen years ago those were the rates. Since the war, however, there have been no rates such as

those, and there is no likelihood of the rates being as low again for many years to come.

I think I said prior to
1910. As I did not expect this question to come up, I have not the figures; but those figures were correct for some years prior to 1910, when the rate averaged about four cents from Fort William to Montreal. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has referred to the possibility of a large canal being constructed from Oswego to New York. It is possible that this canal may be constructed, but I am very doubtful, about that being done. Even if this canal were constructed to a depth of thirty feet as is proposed, there would always be this danger. If, later on, the St. Lawrence river project is carried out, as I hope and believe it will, and it should be a cheaper route, then the more expensive one will have to go out of business. As soon as two routes come into competition, then one that can give the better transportation is the one that is going to take the trade.
I think I have only one more point that I wish to touch on just now, and that is the possibility of boats traversing both the ocean and Great Lakes. I am quite convinced that only a few boats will traverse the ocean and go up to Fort William, for the reason that vessels that cross the ocean cost about three times as much, and because of the more expensive construction and more material in them, they can carry only about two-thirds as much grain. More money is invested, and such boats, having their return cargoes to Montreal where the distributing point must be for some years to come, and not Fort William, will go empty after they have discharged their cargoes at Montreal. They will have to crawl up through those long canals at the rate of four knots an hour, load grain at Fort William and crawl back again. I am convinced that they will never pay. They would also require larger crews.
I was struck with a sentence in an address delivered by Mr. Keefer of Port Arthur, to a body of business men of Montreal in regard to this matter. Many hon. members know that Mr. Keefer is, perhaps, one of the strongest exponents of this project, and in speaking before that body of men, he confessed that it was not likely that any great number of boats would traverse the ocean and proceed to Fort William and Port Arthur to load grain. He said: "A few boats may do so, will do so, but not very many." And I am convinced that that is so. It is really a fatuous dream to imagine that Port Arthur or Fort William is going to become an ocean port.

Like my hon .friend from Fort William and Rainy river, I am a little inclined to think Montreal might make a mistake in opposing this too strongly. I am not going to oppose the St. Lawrence river project; but I would oppose constructing it now, and especially on the strength of resolutions passed and letters written by those who believe they are going to gain eleven cents a bushel. I have sympathy with those who live near the St. Lawrence and believe that as a great international project, this would be a good thing -they will get their power cheaper, the power will in time pay for the project, and Canada will be better thereby. I am willing to listen very sympathetically to what they have to say; but if they are the people who want it, let those people ask for it. I believe the people of the West, if left alone, do not want it now.
Being unprepared and since this question has come up in this way, I shall not have more to say on this subject, but I am pleased that the government are taking the course they are. There are many matters involved, such as the lowering of the water.

PERE (Hochelaga) (Translation) : I have listened, Mr. Speaker, very attentively to the splendid statement of claims made, on behalf of Montreal and its surroundings, by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). I represent, Sir, as you are aware, a large Montreal division most interested in the Maritime import and export trade; I, therefore, deem it my duty to rise in this House and set forth some of the reasons which justify the opposition of my constituents to the St. Lawrence waterway scheme.
The various opinions expressed heretofore, regarding this project are worthy of being considered. Hon. members representing Montreal and the province of Quebec are not alone in disapproving of this scheme and if we look outside of this House, we find that Governor Smith, of New York State, is entirely

St. Lawrence Waterway
opposed to this scheme, so highly extolled within the' last few months, a scheme which has been given widespread publicity in the newspapers, a scheme which is approved, morally at least, by a large proportion of the population of Ontario, and also by the majority of the population of the west. It is true, that this project is of American origin, it was conceived in the states of Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, Missouri, Iowa, Minnesota, the two Dakotas, Montana, Wyoming, Kansas, Nebraska and Colorado. No doubt, the western provinces are interested, however, as it was stated just now, and much to the purpose, by the speaker who preceded me, in these days when all preach economy, the West is not particularly desirious that this scheme should immediately take definite shape.
We have heard the probable cost of this new waterway scheme discussed. I followed attentively, just now, the argument of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who was trying to establish that the cost of this undertaking would not be much more than $250,000,000. Well, Sir, we must, in this House, speak plainly and discuss this question in a businesslike way; to the $250,000,000 which this undertaking is supposed to cost, must be added the interests as long as the system of canals is under construction, and so far as I have been able to judge, there is not one engineer, having made a survey of the ground who is in a position to state in a definite manner that the carrying out of this scheme will take place within a limited time. We are told, however, that the work on the St. Lawrence waterway would last from ten to twenty-five years; if we add to the cost of construction the compound interest, I leave it to you, Sir, to figure out what this scheme will have cost us when completed.
Governor Allan, of the state of Kansas, the greatest champion of this project, states that the United States would, using the St. Lawrence waterway, try and find a market for 200,000,000 tons of merchandise. After having made inquiries from a great number of shippers in my county, I can state positively, that it is absolutely impossible to find any other markets than those at present existing: London, New York, Liverpool, Hamburg and Montreal. Where could this new market be found for 200,000,000 tons of merchandise? That is the question.
We have read, here and there, that the electric power developed, by the St. Lawrence waterway scheme, would be sufficient to defray the cost of this undertaking. We should, Sir,
accept such a statement, only if it can be proven that it is possible to find a market for the electric power so developed. This still remains to be shown.
I am aware that our western farmers have had somewhat to suffer, up to the present, from demurrage charges at the ports where the wheat is unloaded, and this source of complaint will disappear in the future, because we have built quite recently, at Montreal, in my division, a $10,000,000 elevator. This very up to date elevator is designed to store all the wheat that the western farmers may send us, and will facilitate the rapid loading of all the ocean steamers which may come to Montreal during the autumn season, to fetch the wheat destined to the European markets.
I must admit that I place very little reliance in the good-will of our neighbours to the south, when it is a question of business. I am not convinced that our neighbours favour the St. Lawrence waterway scheme with the idea of ensuring to our merchant marine the benefit of this new wheat transportation route. I see but one object which can urge them on to press for the carrying out of this undertaking: it is the development of the water powers. I was reading quite recently, in an American magazine, that Mr. Ten Eyck, an ex-congressman, suggested to his government the building of a new canal extending from Oswego to Troy. Can we reasonably suppose that our friends the Americans would take advantage of the St. Lawrence route and neglect the one extending from Oswego to Troy, and thence to New York by the Hudson river, simply to give proof of their good-will towards us? What our American friends covet above all, is our water powers. We have, up to now, suffered enough owing to the Rush-Bagot Treaty, without further making the mistake of going blindly into such an undertaking by handing to our neighbours advantages which we should keep for ourselves.
All public bodies, Sir, of the province of Quebec, and even the government itself of that province, are strongly opposed to that project. I share their opinion. Montreal is, to-day, a large sea port, which desires to expand, and, within five years, I feel certain, it will extend as far as St. Therese island. If Montreal is, at the present time, considered as one of the five large distributing centres of the world, I fail to see why we should hinder its progress by adopting-even in principle, I might say-a scheme which might have such a harmful result as to injure the great metropolis of Canada.
