I am therefore acting as the spokesman for all the public bodies of Montreal; I am acting as spokesman for all those who, in my division, earn their living in the shipping business; I am acting as spokesman for all those who are truly working in the interest of the Montreal harbour. I approve, without reserve, the opinions advocated by the hon. member for Cha-m-bly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) and I beg the government to act with caution in this affair. And if, some day, a similar project is introduced, I will again side with the hon. members for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) and Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) to request that the Georgian Bay canal scheme be substituted for that of the St. Lawrence waterway.

Representing the constituency which would benefit most by the building of the Georgian Bay ship canal, I wish to say a few words before this discussion is concluded. I am one of those who believe that the commission which is to be named by the government will demonstrate to the satisfaction of our western friends, and to all those who are interested in the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway, the economic impossibility of that project, and that the development of the electrical power on the St. Lawrence is as a matter of fact the real objective of the great propaganda which has been in progress for several years. One of the reasons for the desire to have water-power developed on the St. Lawrence is the necessity that exists to-day for more electrical power in eastern Ontario. I maintain, however, that the building of the Georgian Bay ship canal would supply all the power needed in eastern Ontario, and at a very much cheaper rate than it could be developed along the St. Lawrence. The building of the Georgian Bay ship canal would enable us to develop 1,000,000 horse power, which would be available to eastern Ontario and Quebec, and would also provide an all-Canadian water route, should it ever become necessary, for the grain from the west at a rate every bit as low as that which could be obtained on the St. Lawrence waterway. Furthermore, it would enable Canadians to have absolute control of the grain rates, giving them an all water route to the sea. The Georgian Bay ship canal is a problem that has been discussed in this House for many years, and it has been declared by engineers as perfectly feasible. There is no doubt in my mind that had the United States possessed the same natural advantages, the Georgian Bay ship canal would have been built long ago. Northern

Ontario is on the eve of one of the greatest mineral developments Canada has ever known, The potential wealth of that great north country is just being brought before the world. Within the next ten or fifteen years there will be a greater industrial and mineral development in northern Ontario than has ever taken place in any similar area in the world. The deepening of the Georgian Bay ship canal would give an impetus to the healthy development of the vast natural resources of that country and would no doubt stimulate the development of our rich iron deposits there.
In discussing this problem Mr. W. F. Tye, who has made a thorough study of our waterways, expressed the following opinion:
With tile rapid depletion of the high grade iron ores, and the increase in the cost of coal which mast come from the great waste and rapid exhaustion of the easily mined high grade seams, the great advantages possessed by Pittsburgh and the Ohio valley as a manufacturing centre will disappear. With, the disappearance of the great advantage now enjoyed by Pittsburgh will come Canada's great opportunity.
The construction* of the Georgian Bay canal will develop a very large amount of water power. It is conservatively estimated that the Ottawa and its tributaries will give 3,000,000 horse-power equivalent in power requirements to the mining of 40,000,000 tons of coal per annum. This water power, unlike coal, can never' be exhausted, and with the rapid depletion of the coal and iron in the United States, and with the enormous horse-power of the Ottawa and its tributaries and the low grade iron ores of the Ottawa valley, it is easily possible that in years to come the great manufacturing centre of this continent may be transferred from the Ohio valley to the Ottawa valley. There is no reason why it should not if the people of Canada have the enterprise to make it so For such reasons as this I believe that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal is a national necessity. I do not mean to say that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal will at once transform the Ottawa valley into a great manufacturing centre, but it will "ake l!- possible, as with abundance of iron ore, abundance of the cheapest and best power in the world with a deep draft canal permitting ocean freighters to penetrate into the heart of the Ottawa valley, there seems to be no reason why it should not become in time as great a manufacturing district as any in the world.
The Georgian Bay ship canal would give all the electrical energy required in eastern Ontario for many years to come. Lower down the St. Lawrence, the district of Montreal has all the water-power it will require for the next quarter of. a century.
The development of the St. Lawrence waterways would entail a tremendous expenditure, which would simply augment the stupendous burden this country is already struggling under. The electrical power so generated would have to be transmitted to the United States. As we know, this would lead to the establishment of great industries there, and they having once enjoyed the privilege of receiving

St. Lawrence Waterway
this power we should have to continue to supply their needs right along.
In a statement by Sir Adam Beck, Chairman of the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, on the possibilities of the Ottawa river for power development, made before the Railway committee of the House of Commons in 1912 he said:
The Ottawa river must be the backbone of the supply of electricity to the province of Ontario. We are limited on the St. Lawrence by treaty obligations, and we must depend on one great source of supply, the Ottawa.
We of northern Ontario believe that before any steps are taken for joint international ownership of our great St. Lawrence waterway further study should be given to the merits of the Georgian Bay ship canal. Its construction would mean the development of 36,000 horse-power on the French river and would make it possible for boats to come further inland and supply the coal needs of northern Ontario; it would also serve as an outlet for the pulpwood and timber of that country. In the opinions of those who have studied the development which has already taken place in the north country within the last ten years, it would be a great deal more in the interest of the people of Canada as a whole that the Georgian Bay ship canal should be built in preference to any other similar project.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion on this motion has taken the trend of opposition to the St. Lawrence waterway, and in the case of the last speaker (Mr. Lapierre) of advocacy of the Georgian Bay ship canal. Coming from the centre of the province as I do, it would naturally be expected that I should discuss these rival projects, but I do not intend to do so. I only want to bring to the attention of hon. members that the subject raised this afternoon is the development of water-powers on the St. Lawrence, and I would point out, as I did the other day incidentally, that those who are seeking this development are not concerned in the propaganda which has prevailed in the West for the deepening of the waterway, nor are they behind that propaganda. We believe the time has arrived when electricity is essential to the needs of eastern Ontario, and that the development of this power should not depend upon either the Georgian Bay ship canal or the St. Lawrence waterway route.
The government of Ontario is anxious to develop electricity for the eastern portion of the province, and will undertake to carry out such development at its own cost. That is
the point I want to impress upon the House to-day. Eastern Ontario has been very generous in. its attitude towards the other parts of the province. We stepped aside while hydro-electric power was being developed at Niagara Falls for western Ontario; but we can stand aside no longer-electricity is vitally necessary to eastern Ontario. We have no large industrial centres there, outside of Kingston and a few smaller towns, so the industrial aspect is not of first importance. The primary desire is to have electricity to serve the needs of the settled part of eastern Ontario, principally those of our agriculturists. The development of electrical power on the Georgian bay ship canal would be absolutely useless to us. I do not know what the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) has in mind, but any power development north of the city of Ottawa could not be transmitted to the people of eastern Ontario in an economical way. Ottawa has all the power it wants or will want, but lying along the St. Lawrence river there are very thickly settled parts of Ontario where electricity is required by people living in small towns, and by farmers, and they need it now, not ten, fifteen or twenty years hence. Moreover, the erection of dams for this purpose will not, judging by what the engineers say, interfere in any way with navigation. As an example of this, I would point to the case of the Mississippi River Power Company, which is developing power on the Mississippi by means of a dam, with no resulting interference. I know that some time will be required for the consideration of the question whether or not the canal project is to go on, but I want to impress upon the government that the development of electricity is a matter of great importance to the part of eastern Ontario to which I have referred, and that is a need that the carrying out of the Georgian Bay project or anything else of that kind will not supply. Ontario is anxious to meet this need-
Does my hon. friend say that the building of dams for the supplying of electricity as he suggests will not affect the level of the St. Lawrence river?

Others who have spoken this afternoon have pointed out that they are not engineers; neither am I an engineer. But in 1913 the engineers of the HydroElectric Commission of Ontario stated that the erection of dams would not cause that interference, and I am pointing to an example, that of the Mississippi Power Gompany, which is developing many hundred thousand horsepower.
St. Lawrence Waterway
I am not ready to take the word of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission's engineers.

If any other commission can succeed as well or can get the results which they have obtained, their word should go a long way. I would direct the attention of the government to one other important point, namely, the change of water level along the Great Lakes. The water has gone down not two feet but three or four feet, and the emptying of the drainage and so on is going to be a great menace. The question is a very serious one which the government should take up at once, because the lowering of the water level must expose sewage, with resulting menace to the people of Ontario and of other parts of Canada, and to people of the United States as well. If this condition continues for another year I should not be surprised to see some very serious epidemics in this country.

I	do not wish. Mr. Speaker,
to prolong this debate any further. There is, indeed, very little to add after the splendid speech of the member for Cham-bly and Yercheres (Mr. Archambault). I cannot, however, resist the temptation of protesting against the press campaign which is, at present, being carried on in the United States and Ontario, in favour of the St. Lawrence waterway scheme, I think that the time is ill-chosen-when the people of this country are uniting in a retrenchment campaign to insist on the carrying out of such a project, which would cost hundreds of million dollars. The right hon. Prime Minster (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that it was simply a question of holding an inquiry, so as to judge whether the time was ripe for this undertaking. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) further stated, the other day, that this scheme will never be carried out so long as it has not been established that the level of the St. Lawrence will not be affected, and, he further stated that the rights of all the provinces would be protected. We are continuously being refused necessary improvement for our counties, because Canada is not in a financial position to undertake these improvements, and I cannot, under these circumstances, see the utility of this inquiry, which will certainly cost the country many thousand dollars.
The speakers who have preceded me in this debate have pointed out that each time we had disputes with the United States, they have never been settled to the advantage of Canada ;

the Americans have always succeeded in having their claims acknowledged to our detriment. We must, therefore, be on our guard against such a desire of seeing this project carried out immediately. At all events, Sir, if it was established that an undertaking of this nature is in the interests of Canada, I would rather favour the building of the Georgian Bay canal which would give us an entirely Canadian route. The Georgian Bay canal would create a waterway just as advantageous to the western provinces, and, according to the report of engineers, would facilitate the development of all the water powers of which we are in need, just as well as the St. Lawrence waterway, and it would greatly benefit both northern Ontario and northern Quebec which contain minerals and forests in abundance. The construction of the Georgian Bay canal has been urged for a great number of years, long before we ever heard of the St. Lawrence waterway, and, had it not been for our participation in the war, which brought on a disastrous financial crisis, I am certain that the government would have already begun the construction of that canal. Our financial situation does not permit, at present, the carrying out of that project, which would however be far less costly than the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. It is, nevertheless, a fact that the first great national undertaking that the government will be called upon to carry out, will be the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. All citizens of this country would gladly see the realization of this project which would establish a waterway located entirely on Canadian territory, of which we could be complete owners and not have to share the privileges and responsibilities with our neighbours to the south.
Before closing my remarks, Sir, I would request the government to proceed slowly and with caution and not to carry out the St. Lawrence waterway before it is clearly shown that this project will turn to the advantage of Canada.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): I wish to say a word in support of my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Areham-bault) in his desire that the government should go slowly in entering into any contract with the United States for the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. The history of international canals has not been such that a country, particularly a small country should hasten into a contract with a larger country. The history of the Suez canal and of the Panama canal will show that both the countries through which they were constructed lost control of the territory through which the

St. Lawrence Waterway
canals ran, and it is quite possible that the same thing may happen to us with regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterway if we consent to make the St. Lawrence an international waterway. It is conceivable that at some future time the United States may be at war with some country and that Canada would wish to be neutral but it would be impossible for Canada to obstruct the passage of ships along the St. Lawrence of any country that might be at war with the United States; and vice versa, if Great Britain were at war with Japan, and the United States were friendly with Japan or neutral, I do not see how we could stop their ships from using this international waterway into the Great Lakes. There are many phases of this subject that require very careful consideration before we enter into a contract with the Americans for the construction of this canal. There is no doubt that the canal would be a good thing for the interior of the North American continent. It would mean cheaper transportation and better facilities for all that country. But we have an alternative route in the Georgian Bay canal that would answer the purpose very much better from the Canadian standpoint. My hon. friend the member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) pointed out that there were some 30,000,000 people tributary to the great cities on the Great Lakes.
Has there been any estimate made of the cost of the Georgian Bay canal?

An estimate was made some
years ago, and it was put at about $100,000,-
000.
For what depth of water?
I cannot give my hon. friend the exact depth, but it was to be deep enough for ocean-going vessels.
Twenty-five feet.

The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River pointed out that there were some 30,000,000 people tributary to the territory around the Great Lakes, but those people would be from three to four hundred miles closer to the St. Lawrence outlet by way of the Georgian Bay canal than by way of the St. Lawrence waterway; that is, between Fort William or Chicago and Montreal the Georgian Bay route would be shorter by about three hundred miles than the St. Lawrence route. ,
So far as power is concerned, there is ample power in the Ottawa river for many, many 39
years. It was estimated by the engineers in [DOT] charge of the survey of that waterway that about 1,000,000 horse power could be developed within a reasonable radius of the city of Ottawa. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Ross) was talking of the necessity for power in his district. If he will come to my county he will find he can get power there at $12 per horse-power, which is cheap, if not cheaper than it can be had at any place in Ontario. We can develop power along the Ottawa river cheaper than it can be developed at any point in Canada. The Ottawa has numerous streams emptying into it over the Laurentian range which give a great deal of water power, all tributary to the Ottawa river as well as the power that can be developed on the Ottawa river itself. The Georgian Bay canal could be developed for less than the Canadian proportion of the St. Lawrence waterway, and it would be through all Canadian territory and under our absolute control, and therefore would involve no international complications. I am not saying that the government should rush into the building of the Georgian Bay canal at this moment, but if they are not prepared to build the Georgian Bay canal, they certainly should not commit themselves to the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway at this time. The Georgian Bay canal has been advocated for a great many years, and- plans were prepared very carefully by eminent engineers, and I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I am more converted than ever to the power of the press and of propaganda when the Canadian people have been brought to the point where they will seriously consider the St. Lawrence deep waterway in opposition to the Georgian Bay canal. A few years ago the Georgian Bay canal was the only proposal of this kind that was discussed in this country, before the great West was populated as it is to-day, and before it was producing the wheat it does to-day, but apparently this scheme has been dropped. There has been) no appeal made to the people of the West to support the Georgian Bay canal as a cheap grain route to the East. The advocates of the St. Lawrence waterway have taken up that project and have campaigned vigorously in favour of it throughout the West, distributing literature and doing propaganda work until they have convinced a great number of people in western Canada and the western states that the St. Lawrence deep waterway would be the thing.

They have not convinced
many in the West.

Interim Supply
I trust the members of this House will consider the advisability of recommending to the government, at the earliest possible date the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.
I hope the hon. gentleman recognizes that the sentiment he spoke of in the West in favour of the St. Lawrence scheme does not represent western opinion.

speechtext:
I think I can say in a few minutes all I wish to say on behalf of the government on this motion. The motion is entirely in accord w^th the government's own policy of getting as much information as possible before proceeding in any official way with this great project, and also of having the public as fully informed as possible on all the aspects and bearings of the question. The hon. member (Mr. Archambault) who has introduced the resolution has spoken very emphatically of the many important considerations which this country should take into account before concluding any treaty as far-reaching as a treaty relating to the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway would be, and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr, Cahill) who has just taken his seat has made mention of one_ consideration, namely the international complications that may arise at any time, which also helps to illustrate how important it is that every aspect and possible bearing on the question should be fully considered before anything in the nature of finality is submitted to parliament or is accepted by the government. It is for that reason the government has decided to appoint a national committee to advise on just such matters as have been referred to by hon. members who have spoken. The government recognize? that this is perhaps as large an undertaking as the country has ever been called upon to consider, and our view is there should be a national committee composed of outstanding citizens in whom the public at large will have confidence and to whom the government may look for careful, thoughtful advice in regard to the different aspects of the question. I may say I mentioned this matter a few days ago; my remarks will be found in Hansard of March 17, page 357.
The government has agreed to refer to an enlarged joint engineering board just such questions as the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) has mentioned, namely, the practicability of this scheme, its cost, and particularly the effect upon the river and lake levels. That will be an expert technical board which will report on that particular phase. The government has also appointed a small interdepartmental committee composed of officers of the departments of Railways and Canals, Marine and Fisheries, Public Works, Interior, Trade and Commerce, and Finance, to assemble such information as is contained in the departments
39i
of the government, and also to go carefully into this project from the point of view of the knowledge which government officials have in regard to it. These are all steps in the nature of caution, and if anything more is needed, it will be found in my announcement the other day that the government would not think for a moment of committing the country to any project as great as this, involving so much for both the present and the future as this project does, without first submitting the whole matter to parliament for its consideration.

Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Archambault) replies, there are one or two remarks that ought to be made. In the first instance, it seems to me that, perhaps, it would be wiser if we had not so many declarations from government supporters of absolute opposition to the scheme, when the whole of this matter is to be left very largely in the hands of government employees to say whether the project shall go on or not. If we are to have this investigation, it would be just as well that the engineers investigated it without a threat over their heads or the dice being loaded. In the second instance, it seems rather extraordinary that hon. gentlemen find so much difficulty in having truck and trade with the Americans in connection with a matter which can be very easily made definite, permanent and binding, while on the other hand, they are prepared to hand over the whole of the country's markets to those same gentlemen merely on the face of a gentleman's agreement.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support
the resolution moved by the hon. member for Chambly and Vereheres (Mr. Archambault). This resolution aims at deferring the St. Lawrence waterway scheme.
I congratulate the mover on the splendid outline he has given us on the subject. In my opinion, the government was quite right to appoint a special commission with instruction to look into the report of the International Joint Commission previously appointed. The St. Lawrence waterway project has such far reaching effects. Canada and the United States, at present, have gone so far into the matter that we cannot give' too much study to the reasons invoked by one or the other party. It is quite proper that Canada should be cautious and not venture in such an undertaking without having first foreseen all the consequences. It cannot be denied, this project will entail an enormous expenditure. In the original reports, the engineers claim that the canal system of that part of the St. Lawrence river, between lake Ontario and Montreal, would cost at least $252,000,000; if, however, we take into consideration the whole scheme,-from the Great Lakes to the ocean,-it is quite certain that an undertaking of this nature would reach into the billions of dollars.
Lately, the members of parliament have been receiving numerous pamphlets, some favourable, others unfavourable to the scheme. When this question was first
[Sir Henry Drayton.)
launched, I am convinced that the most interested parties were not citizens of this country, but rather citizens of certain states situated in the neighbouring republic.
In this country, in western Ontario as well as in the western provinces the necessity of such an undertaking has not been fe'.t. No request, that I know of, has been made by those provinces. *
Have we not all the means of communication that we need? Have we not, to-day, numerous and well equipped railways, that have cost a great deal to this country, which, nevertheless, are too numerous, considering our present population? Have we not spent millions of dollars in establishing a canal system on the St. Lawrence? We have canals which are necessary to us, also means of transportation by rail. It is therefore, not in Canada, but rather in the United States that such a request originated. The St. Lawrence waterway would be constructed' from lake Ontario to the ocean, nine tenths of it on Canadian territory, that is to say, that there would only be one tenth of the St. Lawrence waterway which would be located between the United States and Canada. This afternoon, the hon. member for Kingston) (Mr. Ross) claimed that eastern Ontario was deficient in water-powers so as to distribute cheap electricity in its rural districts. If that is what is needed, I think it will be possible to solve the problem in another way and that it will not be necessary to undertake the work on the St. Lawrence waterway. Already, in eastern Ontario, part of the electricity is supplied by the St. Lawrence water powers, such as the Cedar Rapids plant. The Ottawa river can supply that hydraulic power. The development of the water power at Carillon alone would suffice to supply electricity to all eastern Ontario.
This project supported by the government would be to the benefit of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. It would be necessary to dam the Ottawa river at Carillon, so as to develop this source of electric power and place it, at a reasonable figure, on the markets of the province of Ontario as well as the province of Quebec.
h, o great haste exists to carry out an undertaking of such magnitude. We have been at peace for a century with our neighbours to the south and it would be wrong to court occasions for misunderstandings, because this project might have the effect of wiping out the century old "entente mutuelle."
I again state, Sir, I share entirely the opinion so eloquently expressed by the hon.

St. Lawrence Waterway
member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) against the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. On the other hand, if the finances of the country were in a better condition, I do not think there would be a more popular project than the famous Georgian Bay canal.
We have not reached that stage; but I hope in the near future the finances of Canada will allow the government to carry out this project.

In the debate on the Address the suggestion was made by some hon. gentlemen that there had been a great deal of propaganda in the West for the deepening of the St. Lawrence; and there is no doubt in my mind that, if this work were done and at some time in the future we found this country saddled with a debt of $300,000,000 or even more, we might be told that it was western Canada that had launched this scheme. It is well for the House to remember, therefore, just what has been the attitude of hon. members from the West during the past three sessions of parliament whenever this matter has been discussed in the House upon resolution introduced by any member from the city of Toronto. [DOT] So although there may be a good deal of propaganda on behalf of the scheme in the West, especially in my constituency this year, it is as well to remember that at least two years ago there had been already organized in the East an effective propaganda for the same purpose. In order to show that sometimes our friends in the East endeavour to saddle the WTest with the responsibility of initiating the project, I shall quote from an article which recently appeared in the Port Arthur .Chronicle:
Swift Current has the honour of being the first organized municipality in western Canada to take up earnestly the cause of the St. Lawrence deep waterways scheme and place it before the people of western Canada as a feasible and desirable public work.
From Swift Current there recently was issued a little booklet written and published by Mr. Bennett, at his own expense, telling of the benefits that will accrue to the whole country through the development of the St. Lawrence system.
This pamphlet is already beginning to bear fruit as witness the formulation of the first St. Lawrence Canal Association in the West.
Not only should this national waterway be improved for the benefit that it would bring to the grain growers of western Canada, but as a link to bind the separated parts of the Dominion into one whole.
Swift Current is to be commended for the honour it has done itself and Canada, and may nothing stand in the way of the movement spreading from that town to all parts of western Canada.
It would seem from this article that the original propagandists wished to place the
burden and the responsibility for the proposed development upon western Canada, and I am simply rising in my place to emphasize the fact that similar propaganda had already been organized two years before the appearance of this article and before any organization was attempted in Swift Current. I have the honour of representing Swift Current, and it is true that a great many municipalities and boards of trade in my constituency have already expressed themselves in favour of the immediate construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway scheme. But I do not altogether agree with some hon. members who reflect upon the intelligence of these western municipalities and boards of trade, for I do not think it is fair to assert that no investigation into the merits has taken place. We know that the scheme has already been investigated and reported upon. However, I am heartily in accord with the government's decision to institute a fuller and more specific investigation into the merits of the scheme. As showing the absolute necessity for this further investigation, we heard this afternoon an hon. member from my side of the House state that from a certain port in Ontario they could carry grain to Montreal for four cents, while shortly afterwards he was contradicted and told that it would be a matter of thirteen cents.

Is my hon. friend aware that I stated a fact and made an estimate? My fact was that grain is hauled long distances at a cent and a fraction a bushel. Does he deny that fact? As to my estimate, there is no similar condition with which to make a comparison where so many factors would be brought together all tending towards a lower rate. And, this being so, I made an estimate, which may be wrong, and yet it may be right. But does my hon. friend recognize that it was an estimate?

are considering a scheme that would involve the country in the expenditure of millions upon millions of dollars it is not wise to rely upon estimates only; we want to be certain that there is going to be a saving if the scheme is adopted.
I	do not think that Montreal need fear the loss of much traffic, because Montreal is three hundred miles nearer to Liverpool than New York, and if the St. Lawrence waterway development scheme is undertaken there is no doubt that a great deal of freight would pass over it from the sixteen middle western states. That would assist Montreal a great deal; in other words, the volume of business would necessarily be increased. I heartily commend the government for wisely staying their hand in this matter for the time being, especially when there is a demand for economy. I hope the investigation will be full and in detail and that there* will be no political pull or interference in any way so that an investigation may be held which will result in a sane report setting forth to the whole of Canada, the East as well as the West, the benefits that would result from the development of this great scheme.
There is another point that I would like to emphasize. If the proposal originated in the United States and involves chiefly the development of power which they so much need, I do not think the Canadian people should be burdened with the cost of it. But if it can be proved that there are advantages on both sides, that we shall have our share of. the power and that benefit will accrue to the Canadian people as a result of the development, then I hope the time will come when we shall be able to afford the expenditure necessary to carry the project to a conclusion.

I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to take up the time of the House and prolong uselessly the debate on this question. Representing one of the^large electoral divisions of the metropolis of Canada, I deem it my duty to strongly protest against this St. Lawrence waterway scheme. The St. Lawrence river is the source of the prosperity and great development of the city of Montreal, and all which may- affect this river is of vital importance to my fellow citizens. Considering the financial situation of the country, it does seem to me inadvisable to take up just now the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. I must, by the way, congratulate the government for having so clearly understood the present situation and endeavoured to econo-
mize, and, still more economize in order to extricate the country from the chaos in which it was so deeply plunged by the late Tory -Conservative government.
I	wish, Sir, to assure my hon. friend, the member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Arohambault), and my hon. friend the member for Hochelaga (Mr. St. Pere), who also represents one of the large industrial and manufacturing divisions of Montreal, that I entirely share their views and that I shall, like them, strongly oppose this scheme which, in my opinion, would greatly prejudice the interests of the Canadian metropolis, and would, in no way, facilitate the cheap transportation of western wheat. If the Progressives are sincerely striving to better their lot, I think that instead of supporting this scheme, they would be doing far better by supporting the Georgian Bay canal project. This route would greatly shorten the distance between Montreal and Fort William and would allow them to transport .their wheat on better conditions and at reduced insurance rates. I am fully convinced that the whole country would benefit by this last project.
The government should endeavour to develop, first, the projects having a national import before thinking of international undertakings.
The aim of the St. Lawrence waterway scheme, is clearly to seize the water powers of the St. Lawrence river for the greater benefit of the United States. It is the duty of all the representatives of the laTge metropolis of Canada to strive to preserve this asset which the waters of the St. Lawrence represent to us, and prevent them from falling into other hands and thus endanger the future progress of our beautiful city.
I	shall close my remarks, Sir, by congratulating the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres for having drawn the attention of the House to this important question, and for having given proof to the whole country that, to safeguard the national unity, we must not support the schemes which aim at favouring one section only of the country to the detriment of the others, but that we must work together for the common cause, the national welfare.

Mr. Speaker, I have a motion on the order paper dealing with this same subject, and as the matter has been very thoroughly discussed here to-day, I should be very glad, with your permission, to withdraw the motion standing in my name and to confine my discussion of the subject to the present motion.
Two years ago a very admirable report

St. Lawrence Waterway
was presented on this proposed scheme by a commission appointed by both governments. They heard evidence on both sides from the point of view of engineering, finance, traffic and so on. The report subsequently brought in emphasizes the fact that the St. Lawrence is one of the great natural waterways of the world.
The cost of the improvements will be divided between the two countries. The scheme is entirely practicable, according to the engineers, and the cost will be less than that of any other proposed route. The United States government, under the late President Harding, and under the present president in his message at the opening of congress, have taken very strong ground in support of this project. I do not think that anybody in Canada can find fault with the policy of the government to have a further inquiry, provided it be not too long delayed. On the United States side of the inquiry commission will be such men as Herbert Hoover. The report of the last commission has dealt with all phases of this question, but if there is any further information it is in the interest of the country that it be made known. This question should not be approached from any sectional standpoint. What should govern is the greatest good for the greatest number. It is one of the most important economic problems of the North American continent to-day and a right solution of that problem will mean a great deal to the future of Canada, not only eastern Canada but the country as a whole.
For the reasons I have given, and as the government has announced its policy, I support this resolution for the production of papers, and ask leave of the House to with* draw my motion.

Before the hon. member
for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault) addresses the House, if any other hon. member desires to express his views on this question, the time is now. Meanwhile I will put the formal motion: Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) shall have leave to withdraw his motion, No. 26?
Motion agreed to and resolution (Mr. Church) withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, this motion
being for the production of documents and the Prime Minister having assented to it, I shall refrain from answering the arguments made by hon. members who have spoken in the debate, reserving my right to discuss them if
this question should arise on another occasion.
I wish, however, to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). He stated that during my address I said that the construction of a bridge between the city of Montreal and the south shore was more important than the project of the deepening of the St. Lawrence channel. I did not express it that way. What I stated was that it is very difficult for members in the present financial crisis to tell their constituents that many useful and reasonable local projects must be sacrificed because of the state of our finances, and it would be much more difficult in my own case to ask my constituents and those who live in the district of Montreal to refrain from asking the government to contribute directly in the building of that bridge if the government was to go into such an expensive undertaking as the deepening of the St. Lawrence channel. I am sure my hon. friend did not wish to misquote me, but probably the cause of his mistake was that I was speaking in French at the time, and I was not speaking Toronto French.
I also wish to answer one word of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). He compared the St. Lawrence project to the reciprocity pact of 1911 and waxed very indignant about the control of our markets that we were supposed to give to the United States by that pact. I may tell him that by the reciprocity pact we were not giving away any control of any kind to the United States, that in this project we are giving joint control to the United States over a most valuable asset of Canada, and in waxing indignant it was my hon. friend himself who lost control.

Will the hon.
gentleman allow me a question?-whether or not under present existing treaty rights of the United States that country now has the right of navigation in the inland waters?

Yes, there is no
doubt that they have the right of navigation, but they cannot supervise navigation; they cannot build dams, for instance, or make rulings about navigation on the St. Lawrence. But if we were to adopt the project that my hon. friend likes so much we would give to the United States joint control over everything pertaining to the St. Lawrence, that is quite different.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable to appoint a Select Standing Committee to ileal with all matters coming before the House which involve industrial relations.
He said: I am in the happy position of being able to introduce what I think is a non-contentious resolution. We have a number of standing committees in the House dealing with a great variety of subjects, banking, marine and fisheries, mines and minerals, railways and agriculture and so on. There is no committee charged particularly with questions with regard to labour and other matters affecting the relations of the people. It has seemed to me that there are a number of questions that might very well be sent to such a committee. We had last year amendments to the Criminal Code and Immigration Act which were sent to special committees. Some measures are being pressed this year that will have to be dealt with by committees. The government is becoming more and more related to the industrial life of the country. We have now our own national railway system; we are constructing a great many public works; and we have ' 
connections with various contracts which involve the Fair Wage clause and that kind of thing. It seems to me very necessary that there should be every facility given for discussion and understanding of these various questions in this House. We have been urging upon labourers and employers alike that, wherg possible, constitutional and parliamentary methods should be adopted in solving these problems. I take it, then, that we should have the machinery for a very full consideration of these questions. I have no intention whatever of arguing the case tonight. It seems to me the proposition itself is eminently a reasonable one. If the farmers feel in connection with their agriculture that they ought to have a committee, we in the Labour group feel that we might very well have a similar committee to deal with labour questions. I offer this as a suggestion to the government and the House, and would be very glad if the government could see its way to accept it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) was kind enough to mention to me before the House met this year that it was his intention to introduce a resolution of this kind, and he will recall I expressed to him the view that I hoped he would do so. I see no objection whatever to the object of the resolution. I would like, however, to point out to my hon. friend that we already have a very large number of select standing committees. I think the number of select standing committees in our parliament, is about twice the number in the British House of Commons, ilthough, of course, we have not more subjects or subjects of larger magnitude to consider. Each additional committee means something in the way of additional expense, not a very great expense to be sure, but nevertheless it does entail an extra clerk and stenographer or two, and other additional expense.
The government has been considering this matter and we feel that possibly the object my hon. friend has in view would be met, and a still larger object attained, if we were to consolidate two of the committees that are now separate committees, and form a new select standing committee on industrial relations; broadened, however, so as to make it not a standing committee on industrial relations only, but a committee also on international relations. Of recent years the importance of both of these classes of questions has very greatly increased. Members

Soldier Settlement
of the House will notice that more and more time has been taken up ever since the war with the discussion of international questions, such important matters for example as the one referred to in a question asked by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) relating to the Singapore base. There have been many questions relating to the matters that came before the Imperial Conference, and I venture to say that every few weeks we shall be discussing in this House some question of international import. It may well be that a select standing committee to consider these international questions would serve a very useful and helpful purpose. True, any subject can be referred under the rules of the House to almost any committee if there is relevancy at all, and so the House is not precluded from having any matter considered in a select standing committee, but there is an advantage, when committees are being chosen, in placing on each committee those members of the House who are likely to have a special interest in and a special knowledge of the questions to be discussed. I think the combination of industrial and international problems would be a very proper one. International questions deal in very large part with industrial matters, and certainly our industrial problems are becoming more and more international in character. To add a new select committee would require an amendment to Rule 10 of the House. That would require a couple of days' notice. But if members of the House generally approve of the idea, the government would be prepared to bring in an amendment to the rules suggesting a consolidation of two of the select standing committees and the formation of a new select standing committee on industrial and international relations. If that meets with the approval of my hon. friend I have no objection on behalf of the government in sanctioning the resolution as it stands.

SOLDIER SETTLEMENT Mr. W. J. WARD (Dauphin) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the abnormal deflation in the value of all farm products which has taken place since the year 1920 and which has been reflected particularly in the economic position of the returned men who have gone on the land under the provisions of the Soldiers Land Settlement Act, renders it imperative that immediate consideration be given to the question of a substantial reduction of their capital debt. And that a committee of this House be appointed to whom this matter may be referred with instructions to review the situation and report to parliament at the earliest possible date this session.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I introduce this
motion only after having made a most exhaustive survey of the situation as it exists in my constituency, and also, since coming to Ottawa, after having surveyed the question from the broader aspect in discussions with various members of this House. I made that survey of my constituency and of other portions of Manitoba in company with, not only the local supervisors, but the district supervisor for Manitoba. Therefore, I introduce this question with a full realization of all that is involved in making a physical revaluation. If I were to suggest the measure that, I believe, would be in the best interest of the soldiers of my constituency and of the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada, I would advocate a complete cancellation of the whole account. My reason for making that statement is this. After having made a survey of my constituency and after having secured figures from the various departments, I found that this condition prevailed in my constituency. There had been-I use the term "had," because I do not contend that the same amount is invested now-invested in that constituency through the Soldier Settlement Board, $2,750,000. Of that sum, on the 30th September last, abandonments had taken place to the amount of $600,000, of which the government or the board had been able to salvage only 18 per cent. If abandonments should- continue for another two years at the same rate at which they have taken place during the last twelve

Soldier Settlement
months, we shall have lost all the returned soldiers but 15 per cent. That is the situation in my constituency. Therefore, if the abandonments continue at the same rate for another two years, we shall then be in exactly or almost the same position as we would be if we cancelled the entire account to-day. I am not, however, asking for cancellation of the entire account; I am asking for revaluation. Two years ago when a special committee sat considering these matters, I was one of the few members of this House who strongly advocated revaluation then. I think the chairman of that committee, whom I see in the House to-night, will recall that almost daily I waited upon him and urged that revaluation should take place; that I was sure it would have to take place some time. I think we have arrived at the time when revaluation is the only possible solution if we intend to retain the soldiers on the land. I secured some figures from the department at Ottawa on the question of abandonment and so forth, and I will give the figures for all the provinces in the Dominion:

This makes an average of 18-1 per cent of abandonments. Nor does this tell the . whole story. In discussing this question with the chairman of the Soldier Settlement Board at Ottawa the other day, I learned that the field supervisors, in submitting their reports, classified their soldiers something like this. There is a class that they call "good;" there is another class that they call "fair;" there is another class that they call "doubtful," and there is a fourth class that they term as "likely to quit." In the class that is likely to quit there were 12 per cent. If you add the 12 per cent of those who are likely to quit to the 18 per cent of those who have already quit, we have 30 per cent that have practically abandoned their farms. In the West we hear a great deal about mixed farming; in fact, to-day it is held out as the panacea for all our ills, and many of the soldiers in my constituency have attempted to readjust their position and tried mixed farming, but it has not stopped the exodus.

I have under my hand a report from the municipality of Lakeview which, I think, is in the constituency of Neepawa. In the Lake-view municipality there were settled 101 soldiers under the Soldier Land Settlement Act, of whom 53 have already abandoned their farms. One of the supervisors in my constituency advised me, just before I left for Ottawa, that 100 soldiers had left his district in the last twelve months.
I do not intend to go into this matter at any length to-night. Other members are present who, I know are anxious to say a few words on this particular question. I feel that with the situation as it exists to-day. there will be very little opposition to the matter of appointing a committee of this House, and we shall have an opportunity of discussing the question when the report of that committee, if one should be appointed, is submitted to the House. As the hour may be late when we conclude this debate, I do not intend to say more than merely to introduce this question, and I may have a few remarks to make in closing the debate. I would point out to the government, however, that if the purpose of the Soldier Settlement Act, namely, to establish the soldiers on the land, is to be effective, something must be done to build up the morale, to stimulate the hope and to improve the psychological condition of the soldiers. If something is not done, I am convinced that within two years from now, in Manitoba at least, we shall have lost practically all the soldiers.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman gone into many of the reasons why, say, 18 per cent of our soldiers have left the land?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In making the survey that
I mentioned at the outset of my remarks, I visited personally in the neighbourhood of one hundred soldiers' farms, went into their homes, talked the matter over with them and asked them why they were not able to make their farms pay. The question is simply one of high cost of production and low-priced products. Another reason that might be mentioned is that in many of the districts the soldiers were settled on land on which they should never have been settled.
I have here the prices that were paid for land in the various provinces of Canada, and it may be interesting to hon. members to learn just how much was paid on the average in the West. In British Columbia the average price was $54 per acre; in Alberta $18 per acre; in Saskatchewan $17.50 per acre; in Manitoba $20 per acre; in Ontario $38, and

Soldier Settlement
in Quebec $30, the average over the whole lot being $22.50. In Manitoba, where the average price was $20.25, I have no hesitation in stating my opinion that no honest and practical man would	value	any of the land sold	to thesoldiers at	more	than $10	per acre.	I amconvinced of that. I believe that the land was	sold	to these	men at	pricesthat were	at	least 50	per cent	more
than should have been charged. I do not want to charge anything like wrong doing, because everything was inflated at that time. But there is no doubt whatever that these men paid altogether too much for the land they got. Land was greatly inflated then, and very high prices were paid for stock also, cows, for example, were selling then at $125 each, and I know of several teams of horses that were bought for returned men at as high as $500 and $550 apiece. It was exceedingly unwise, in the first place, to buy stich expensive horses for the returned men going into the backwoods and on the frontiers; and high prices were paid for cows that are to-day worth not more than $20 apiece. This accounts largely for the failure of these men to meet their payments.
I want to reiterate, because of its importance, the fact that while the financial insolvency is a very serious matter, what I call the psychological insolvency is not less serious. Let me give an illustration of what I mean.
I visited a home about a year ago last fall, and although the returned man himself was somewhat downhearted, at the same time his wife appeared to me to be rather elated; she had some hope of being able to augment the family budget, since she had decided to go into the raising of ducks. She raised 75 ducks last year, a beautiful flock of birds, and in the fall she crated them and shipped them to Winnipeg. In return she received a cheque that netted her 22 cents apiece for these ducks. You can imagine the pscychological effect of this circumstance upon that soldier's wife. Only the year before she had entertained high hopes of being able to help the family by providing the means for obtaining the necessary clothes and groceries which they would require. And this is what happened. I say, Mr. Speaker that the psychological conditions that surround the lives of a great many of the returned soldiers are such that it is impossible for them to carry on. I am sure that the House and the government will show in some way their appreciation of what the soldiers have done for us. Do not let us forget these men who went overseas and endured a virtual hell to save
loved ones, homes and country and the lives of others who stayed at home fortifying ourselves against the days that were to come.
I think that this parliament owes it to the returned men to show them every consideration which it possibly can. I will not take up more of the time of the House, but I beg to bring my remarks to a close with an expression of hope that the government will see its way clear to appoint a committee to go fully into the matter; and I shall be glad to give any information that I may possess, as I am sure other hon. members will be only too ready to do.

speechtext:
I wish to add a few words to what has been already said by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward). I think the hon. member is in a better position than any other hon. gentleman to speak for the province of Manitoba. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this is a subject, one might say, of almost tragic importance, and I desire the House to be fully seized of the situation and to know that all is not well with the soldier settlers. We have heard some glowing reports in regal'd to this matter, and while I do not suppose that they have been intentionally misleading, nevertheless it seems to me that this House should be made aware, as it is not, in my opinion, of the precise situation in reference to a great many of the returned soldiers out on their farms in the prairie provinces where I am acquainted. No doubt we have had right intentions so far as our dealings with the returned soldiers have been concerned. We are proud of the fact that no other country has done so much for those who went to the war as has the Dominion of Canada. However, we must not allow ourselves to feel that we have done all that we can do and that everything is all right. If anything can be done more than we have done we should seriously consider the matter and ascertain in what way we can relieve the situation of the returned men.
An hon. member on the other side of the House asked why the returned farmer soldiers had got into the condition in which they found themselves to-day. Well, it is not very difficult to answer that question. The House is continually hearing stories about the difficulties that confront the whole agricultural population of the country at the present time. We know that farmers who own their own farms, their own stock and implements, are experiencing great difficulty in keeping their heads above water, and when we reflect that the returned soldiers had to face a handicap when they went upon the land, I do not think we shall be surprised to find them in straitened circumstances to-
Soldier Settlement

day. There came to my office to-day a gentleman of ability, a man who had spent a number of years in the war. He told me that on his return he thought at first that he would find comparatively little difficulty in settling down; but, he added, so soon as he tried to buckle down he discovered that he could not, and it was quite a while before he was able to get into his stride. That is something that must be taken into consideration. We must remember, too, that a great many of these men were not highly experienced agriculturists, and they went upon the land because it offered an attraction: they naturally wanted to live an independent life and to earn an income that would support them. When the soldiers began to settle on the land in large numbers in 1919 and 1920, at the time the great bulk of the land and the stock and implements were bought, everything was at the highest price; things were higher then than they have been in the last fifteen or twenty years. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I am going to read some extracts from a few letters I have received. These letters are not anonymous; they are all signed, and while I will not give the names, I may say that the writers are all prominent business men in different towns in the province of Manitoba. The first is from the town of Eriksdale:
In this district the settlers are having great difficulty to content themselves to stay with the farm as they realize that it is going to be a hard proposition to keep up these payments, for the number of years they will be obliged to, in order to clear themselves of the debt which is hanging over them.
The next comes from the town of Carman:
Settlers are on the poorer land as the board would not purchase the best land at from $70 to $100 an acre. They will have a hard time paying for the land unless they go in for mixed farming, as it is very light.
I have another one from Eriksdale:
There are very few if any soldier settlers in this neighbourhood making much progress as the majority started when prices were at tlieir peak.
Another comes from Dominion City:
Unless conditions are made much better for the farmer the land is not worth any more now than it was in 1913. Unless a change is made soon the soldiers can never make it pay, as they had to pay far too much to get a start.
The last one comes from Minnedosa:
I yield to no one in my interest in the establishment of returned men on the farm, and speaking generally they have paid 33 per cent too much for everything.	-
This is signed by Hugh M. Dyer,-General Dyer, who made a name for himself in the war and who I am sure is a friend of the soldier. I have read these letters to show what is the general opinion all over the prov-
ince of Manitoba as to the condition in which the farmers find themselves.
It is difficult enough for the soldiers, but the municipalities are suffering too. They are not able to collect taxes from these lands. As a result, in many districts in the province where soldiers have been settled, the schools are being closed and the children are receiving no education. We also find considerable debts due to the hospitals for treatment given soldier settlers and their dependents. I have a list before me of the various municipalities in Manitoba, with the number of soldier settlers and the number of those who have been forced to abandon their farms; but I will not deal with this because the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) has already given the percentages and I need not duplicate his remarks. But I find that the unpaid taxes in Manitoba-and this is not a complete list by any means- amount to about $42,000, while unpaid hospital bills run to over $3,000.
In order that the House may understand some of the circumstances that surrounded the purchasing of land for soldier settlers, let me give the figures respecting a quarter section. The land was obtained originally from the provincial government in 1906 for $720; in 1917 it was again sold for $1,760; but the Soldier Settlement Board paid $4,500 for the quarter section-a rise from $720 to $4,500. There is no doubt about these figures, and I can verify them at any time. If the original owner bought the land for $720, how in the world does anyone expect a soldier settler to be able to pay $4,500 for it, buy his stock and implements, and make a living? It is an utter impossibility, and the quicker the man gets off the land the better.

speechtext: What province was that in?

speechtext:
Manitoba. I think there
should be a thorough investigation. I am not blaming anyone for graft or other dishonest dealing. It is well known that the soldier settlers came into possession of their land, and bought their stock and implements when everything was at the peak. As I have already said, the farmer without any encumbrances on his land finds it difficult enough to make ends meet; but these poor men are up against an impossible proposition. When I think of some of these soldier settlers with their wives and families in the hewer districts enduring hardships and confronted with many trials and difficulties, and then remember what the men did for us when the Empire was fighting for its very existence, I feel that we in our turn cannot do too much for them, and I would ask this House to institute a thorough investiga-

Soldier Settlement
tion into all the circumstances, because I do not believe for a moment that our people wish to see the slightest injustice done to these veterans who were willing to sacrifice their lives that we might be free.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SELECT STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having a goodly number of returned soldiers in my constituency, and knowing the condition in which many of them now find themselves, I cannot conceive of any resolution with which I am more heartily in accord. I will not dwell at great length on this question because it has already been pretty well covered. I believe the scheme was perfectly sound in its inception, but unfortunately it was started at a very bad time, at a time when land, horses, implements and everything else were at the peak and just starting to decline in value.
I have visited some of these returned soldiers, and they have appealed to me for support. A very great majority of them are very economical and hard-working men, and many of them are not as strong physically as they were before they went overseas. I have one man in mind now whom I visited last fall. He had a tidy place, and everything looked thrifty. He was not a strong man physically, in fact he was in a nervous condition, and probably he will never be as strong again as he used to be; and yet he was doing wonders, working long hours. He had built a cowshed of poles and straw, and although there was only about $45 worth of lumber in it, the result was a credit to any man. He was doing all that any farmer could possibly do to make a living, yet he was in financial difficulties.
In some cases the land purchased was not of good quality. The man I refer to wa3 fortunate in having a sound knowledge of land and was able to pick a very choice quarter section, but where the men were not good judges they had to depend on inspectors of the Soldier Settlement Board to pick out their farms. The board itself at the outset had to take on untried men, and in some cases these men [DOT] were not properly qualified for the duties required of them. Later on, I believe, this trouble was overcome, but in the meantime a goodly number of soldiers were placed on land that was not just suitable for farming. I do not know that anybody in particular was to blame, but that was the situation.
These men did their very best for us, they served us, as has been well said, faithfully and without stint. While some of us were able to profit by the war, these men sacrificed everything, and I should very much like
to see this resolution taken seriously in order that we may help such deserving cases. Difficulties lie in the way, but I do not think they are insurmountable, and if we could have a revaluation made of the land and property it would give these men fresh hope and renewed courage to try to hold on to their farms. Otherwise they will slip away from this country the same as the 30 per cent already referred to. I have some letters also from returned soldiers somewhat similar to those read by my leader (Mr. Forke) but 1 do not think it is necessary for me to place them before the House. I wish to give the resolution my most hearty commendation and support.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say just one or two words in support of this motion, and also to make a suggestion. Anything that goes to make a farm-land, equipment and stock -is of value eventually in proportion to the value of products which can be sold from that farm. Land may be sold, and possibly be resold, at a high price, but if a man has bought it and intends to make it his home, to live on it for twenty-five years and pay for it, he must pay for it eventually out of the value of his products, and it is the low value of the products in comparison to the capital debt on the farm that has largely brought about the present situation.
The act was orginally, I believe, a good act, but with the changed conditions its provisions became inadequate to meet the situation. Of course none of us expected at that time that there would be such a tremendous deflation of values, particularly in the comparative values-that is, the purchasing values-of farm products. I am not attaching blame to anyone, nor should any blame be attached. The matter is one in which all members of the House are equally interested, and I think, equally sympathetic. Two years ago we had hoped that the difficulty was met; we attempted honestly to meet it. But since then ^matters .have developed and the soldiers' position has become worse. As the conditions change and as matters become worse we must change our act, if necessary, to meet the existing circumstances, just as we tried to do two years ago. However, I do not intend to speak of that so much as to point out one or two of the complexities of this problem which make it necessary that some such committee as has been suggested be appointed if the problem is to be dealt with intelligently, as it must be if it is to be dealt with satisfactorily.
There is the question, for instance, whether such readjustment of the capital debt should be retroactive, and if so to what extent, Some men have paid a good deal on their lands and others have paid very little, so the question whether it shall or shall not be retroactive must be given consideration. There is also the question of the basis of the revaluation, whether it shall be a physical revaluation or a revaluation by percentage. I think we pretty nearly came to the conclusion in 1922 that a physical revaluation was almost an

impossibility, that is, to send men to every farm to value them in accordance with their respective market prices. In some parts of the country there is no market price because there is no demand for land and no land exchanging hands. But in any case the expense involved in making a complete and systematic investigation of every parcel of land and of all the equipment and stock on these parcels of land would be almost prohibitive. Further, it would to a certain extent discriminate against the careful settler in favour of the settler who was not so careful. The more careful a settler was, the better he farmed his land and the better the condition in which he kept his stock and equipment, the less would be the deflation in value, so that such a physical revaluation would to a certain extent discriminate in favour of the careless settler.
The question also comes up as to localities. There is no doubt that certain localities were not well adapted to farming and that there is greater deflation in those localities than in others. On the other hand, if the percentage basis was taken, if you simply reduced the capital debt by a given percentage, I suggest that you might have to adopt some kind of sliding scale percentage, based possibly to some extent on the locality and also to some extent on the years during which the purchases were made.
These are the complexities of the problem, and they have to be faced. In the first place, we have to safeguard the men who did so much for us, because after all it is not merely a matter in their case of dollars and cents; it is not simply a colonization problem. We endeavoured to assist these men, to put them on a better footing than that on which they would have been had they not taken out these loans-that was our purpose, in addition, of course, to our attempt to increase production through that method of colonization. The suggestion I would make, then, would be this. If the government see fit to accept this resolution, and I most certainly hope they will, I suggest that the reference should be somewhat widened. The resolution itself would refer to a committee simply the matter of a decrease in the capital debt. Now, that is involved with other matters; it is almost impossible to consider a subject of that kind by itself.	I would therefore, with the permission of the House and of the mover of the resolution (Mr. Ward), move to amend it by inserting after the word "matter" in the second last line the following words:
"together with any other question relative to the operations of the Soldiers Land Settlement Act,"

Soldier Settlement
The last paragraph would then read:
And that a committee of this House be appointed to whom this matter, together with any other question relative to the operations of the Soldiers Land Settlement Act, may be referred,-
And so on, I hope that the mover of the resolution will agree to the amendment and that the House will adopt the resolution as amended.

Mr. Speaker, I asked one or two questions a few minutes ago, but not with the intention, as I stated then, of opposing the motion now before the House. It has my heartiest support; I honestly believe that something should be done to ameliorate the conditions of these men now upon the land, I agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) that perhaps the motion does not go far enough to provide for an inquiry, into all the circumstances, and I question whether the motion in its original form might not bring upon the country a greater expense than the saving to the soldiers.
There is no doubt that many of these men bought land when the land was at the peak price. Generally speaking the land was largely in the hands of local men whose honesty or dishonesty was well known throughout the community, and I think that on the whole they did the best they could under the circumstances. Since that time, not only in the West but in some portions of eastern Canada as well, the conditions have changed, and there is very good reason for the proposing of a motion of this kind at this time. We have an example in this respect that our friends to the left may not have noticed; the Dominion of New Zealand is at present engaged in revaluing all the lands sold in that country to returned soldiers. These lands were sold on a basis of a term of purchase of thirty-five years, a much longer term and with much smaller payments than applied in the case of our men, who were supposed to make a payment of ten per cent before the land came into their possession at all. New Zealand did not experience the boom that we had during the war period, for reasons which it is unnecessary for me to enumerate to-night, but they have found it necessary to revalue all these lands. I am thoroughly prepared to support a motion of this kind, whether moved by the hon. member who proposed it (Mr. Ward) or by any other member of the House, and I think that in doing so I am voicing the opinion not only of the group which immediately surrounds me but of every returned soldier in the House. I have some doubt whether it would be wise or unwise to make this
retroactive; I have very grave doubts whether it should be on a percentage basis; but these are matters that should be threshed out by a committee of this House, and when we all put our heads together, those who are in favour of any action along this line and those who are opposed, we can no doubt suggest some plan whereby we can give these men presently on the land by our volition, not their own perhaps, fair play in this matter. I am in favour of a committee. I am opposed to a commission because I think it would take too long, cost too much, and not be entirely in the interests of those we desire to serve. So I support most heartily the amendment of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).
