Mr. Speakei I wish to associate myself with those who are supporting this resolution. I prefer the resolution as amended because I think it covers the ground better, but I feel that I would hardly be doing my duty if I did not support this motion for a committee of the House. I have discussed this matter with the returned men in my constituency. There are many there who are in financial difficulties, as there are in other places. I visited them personally and talked with them, in order to get their viewpoint. The resolution asks for a revaluation. I am not particular myself whether it is a revaluation or a percentage cancellation of the debt. I think that could best be worked out by a committee of this: House, after going into the matter thoroughly..
I might, however, give the views of many different men I have talked with. I asked for - their ideas regarding a percentage cancellation of their debt, simply because I was led to believe from the former inquiries held that a revaluation would be very difficult. I asked them how much of their debt they felt should be cancelled in order for them to make good under present conditions, and their ' opinions varied all the way from thirty to fifty per cent as the percentage to be cancelled before they would be able to pay up and hold their land. But the committee would be able to determine that better than I could from the information I have.
I realize that from whatever angle this, problem is attacked there will be difficulties. There are difficulties in a revaluation. If we have a percentage cancellation the man who has made the best and most intelligent effort, and who has been perhaps the most industrious, would be penalized more or less unless the cancellation were made retroactive. The soldier himself might be blamed in some cases, but on account of the deflation in
Soldier Settlement

values it is only the man who has had good experience and is very favourably situated who could have made good. I feel that we were all to blame more or less. I felt quite pleased when the government first decided to undertake this land settlement scheme. We needed the soldiers as producers, and we needed to find a place for our soldiers returning from the war, and this offered an opportunity. In some cases men have undertaken farming operations without proper experience, but I think that conditions generally are to blame more than anything else. I do not think that the men who were locating these soldiers, in many 'cases at all events, were dishonest or did anything dishonourable, but conditions are so bad that we must look into them, and I think that a committee of the House is the. best way to deal with the question, and that is why I support the suggestion. The government will lose in any event. If they wait for the soldier to leave the land, discouraged as he would be, the government will lose in that way. If the soldier stays on the land and cannot pay, the government will lose in that case. So we have to make the best of conditions as they are, and it is for us to do what we can to provide a remedy to do the best we can for these men. For these reasons I am in favour of a committee being appointed.

Mr. Speaker, though I do not pretend to know the provisions of the Land Settlement Act in detail, still I feel that I should say a few words on this occasion. As the House is aware, the administration of the Land Settlement Act is vested in the hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, but at the present time my hon. colleague (Mr. Robb) has such important duties to discharge as Acting Minister of Finance that I felt perhaps the House would pardon me if I rose and said a few words on this occasion on behalf of the government.
The debate which has taken place has been in more than one regard informative. It has brought home to a very large number of members of this House some conditions not at all favourable which prevail amongst the land settled soldiers. The act which was passed gome years ago was passed unanimously by this parliament with the best of intentions. At that time it was foreseen and expected and hoped that soldiers who decided to avail themselves of the privileges of the act would in time succeed in their new avocations. It is well to remember that at that time the price of land in Canada was at its peak, and almost without a moment's warning, after

a large number of soldiers had availed themselves of the provisions of this act, the price of cultivated land in Canada started to decline. To-day conditions for agriculturists generally throughout Canada are far from being favourable, as we are all ready to admit; but what of the condition of the soldier who has to bear in addition the burden of the interest on a very large loan which he has received at the hands of the government? Taking all in all, it is impossible to say that the act has been a failure. In my opinion the act has been a success. It is almost miraculous that such a small proportion of the men who have entered upon this scheme have decided to abandon it or have been unable to carry on. Loans, generally speaking, have been repaid in a very respectable measure. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), has pointed out, I think perhaps better than any other hon. member who has spoken on this subject, the course that would likely be adopted as the more favourable, both from the point of view of the soldier settler himself and the country. My hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Ward) is asking that a committee be appointed for the purpose of investigating the subject and reporting to the House for its action. Every session since the war ended, the House has appointed a committee to deal with soldiers' affairs generally, with the exception of last year. Two years ago the committee generally known as the committee on Pensions and Re-establishment sat for many weeks, and not only examined the question of re-establishment and the question of pensions, but also dealt extensively with the question of land settlements, and submitted to the House a report on which certain action was taken, relieving in a certain measure the bad lot of the land settled soldiers. Last year no committee wtas appointed. This year the question of appointing a committee of a like kind has been under consideration by me for a number of weeks.
I have so far not made up my mind whether such a committee would be indispensable or not. All that has been said this evening by hon. members who addressed the House would lead me to believe that a committee of the kind should also be appointed this year. Moreover the final report of the royal commission appointed to investigate and report upon the question of re-establishment will be submitted to the House within, I understand, two or three weeks, if I am to rely on the communications that I have received from the chairman of that commission. It will probably be necessary to appoint a committee

Soldier Settlement
when this report is laid on the Table of the House, in order to devise truly the proper legislation which will be indicated on the face of that report. I would make a suggestion to my hon. friend who has moved the resolution (Mr. Ward), and the hon. members who have supported it. If he will allow his motion to stand or to drop, I will undertake to move for the formation of a committee .within a few weeks, in order that both subjects I have referred to-that is the one discussed this evening and also the final report of the commission-may be submitted to this committee. The investigation should not take very much time. I believe that if the committee were appointed, say in three or four weeks, it would be all that is necessary in order to discharge the duties that will be expected from it.
Some reference has been made, Mr. Speaker, by the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) to the duty which this country owes to returned men. I do not hesitate for one moment to concur with the remarks which have fallen from his lips. I remember once in my capacity as medical man I had given my care and attention to a friend of mine who had been ill for a number of weeks, and happily nature came to my rescue very considerably and my friend recovered entirely. After a little while he sent me a note in which he said, "I wish you would tell me what that part of my debt towards you consists in, that which you call your doctor's bill. As far as the other part of my debt is concerned, I can never discharge it." I think the country may make the same statement to the returned men. The part of our debt to these returned men which is not counted in dollars and cents can never be discharged adequately. So far as I am concerned, I will in all possible ways assist my hon. friend who has moved this resolution, and if he will allow the matter to stand for two or three weeks, until we get the report of this commission, I shall move this committee, and all the subjects referring to the soldiers may then be gone into fully.

Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (West Edmonton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is a bill
Half-breed Scrip

to amend section 20 of chapter 25 of the statutes of 1921. We discussed this matter two sessions ago and it is up again at this session. I introduced the bill last session, but it did not reach the second reading. Objection has been tatken to the amendment that was passed to the Criminal Code in 1921, because at the time it was passed, certain half-breeds on the borders of northern Alberta and the provisional district of Mackenzie had made somewhat strenuous efforts to secure an adjustment or redress in connection with what they claimed was a very severe grievance. Scrip was issued to halfbreeds residing in the Northwest Territories, that is in the district of Athabaska, in the years 1900 and 1903. P.C. No. 918, passed on the 6th May, 1899, reads:
The practice heretofore followed in satisfying such claims under that provision has been.
1.	To issue scrip, redeemable in land, to the extent of $160, to each half-breed head of a family, on proof of residence in accordance with the terms of subsection aforesaid.
That is subsection (f) of section 90 of the Dominion Lands Act.
2.	To issue scrip, redeemable in land, to the extent of $240. or scrip entitling the grantee to 240 acres of land of the class open to homestead entry, at the option of the claimant, to each child of a half-breed head of a family on proof of such residence.
The minister therefore recommends that as to the half-breeds of the territory to be covered by the proposed treaty the following policy be adopted:
1.	That every half-breed occupier of land in the said territory be confirmed in possession to the extent of 160 acres.
2.	That scrip, redeemable in land, to the extent of $240, or at the option of the grantee, scrip entitling the grantee to 240 acres of land of the class open to homestead entry be granted to each half-breed found to be permanently residing in the said territory at the time of the Indian Treaty and not to have previously received scrip in extinguishment of his claim.
The Indians of the territory were met by the treaty by which they still receive treaty money and they also got the reserves. As regards the claims of the half-breeds, due to the fact that they were persons with mixed white and Indian blood, their Indian claim was extinguished through the issue of scrip, redeemable in land. A number of those scrips were issued in that territory, and it is claimed that several hundreds of persons living in the northern boundary of Alberta and in the Northwest Territories, were defrauded in connection with the transfer of scrip and its location. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) was Prime Minister of Canada, he visited the city of Edmonton in November, 1920. On the 11th November, a delegation of two half-breeds met him in the 
Macdonald hotel at Edmonton and presented this petition.
The petition of Philip Atkinson and Alexa Lafferly humbly showeth:
That your petitioners are persons of mixed white and Indian blood, residing at or near Fort Resolution, in the province of Alberta, and that your petitioners have been delegated by a number of persons of mixed white and Indian blood, residing in the environments of Fort Resolution, Fort Smith and Fort Chippewyan, seeking redress for what they believe to be a real grievance and to ask that justice be done them.
The next paragraph goes on to state that between the years 1900 and 1903 scrip was issued to a certain number of persons under certain conditions; and the third paragraph reads:
That unscrupulous speculators following in the wake of the commission entrusted by the hon. Minister of the Interior with the delivery of such certificates or half-breed scrip and, taking shameful if not even criminal advantage of the illiteracy and ignorance of the half-breed, purchased such scrip from the holders, paying-
And this is the point.
-paying therefor a proportion of the agreed purchase price, and agreeing to pay the balance, together with the expenses of the vendor in travelling to and from the land office at such time as the vendor might be called upon by the purchaser to come to the Dominion Lands Office and file upon the parcel of land located and selected by the purchaser. Many of the unscrupulous purchasers, instead of bringing the vendor to the land office and paying him or her the expenses of such trip, together with the balance of the agreed purchase price, by fraud, perjury, subornation of perjury and forgery procured other persons to appear at the land office and represent themselves to be the persons named in the scrip, and to file upon the land selected or located by the purchaser, and to forge the name of the real vendor to transfers and other documents in connection therewith, thereby committing a fraud upon His Majesty's government and a fraud upon the vendor. That in the north country in the neighbourhood of Forts Resolution, Smith and Chippewyan, there are several hundred half-breeds who have been defrauded and with respect to whose scrips His Majesty's government has been defrauded. And your petitioners pray that a commission be appointed to inquire into-
And so on. The then Prime Minister took the petition with him to Ottawa and it was turned over for attention to the Department of the Interior, the minister in charge at that time being Sir James Lougheed. A reply was sent from the department signed by Mr. Cote to the effect that requests of this kind for investigaion had been presented to the department on several occasions previously and that the department had not seen fit to take action. It was said in the letter:
The question has been before the department on several occasions in the past, and in view of your petition has again been considered. The scrip certificates issued in satisfaction of half-breed claims and scrip notes issued by the department were delivered to the grantees personally, and it is not considered that

Half-breed Scrip
the department can be held responsible for subsequent, action taken in connection with the location of the scrip; and if there were any fraud perpetrated' in connection therewith it was open to them to take ordinary proceedings before the proper courts.
Now, the department having taken the stand that they had no further responsibility, and that such a length of time had elapsed that it would be difficult to dig up evidence that could be relied upon, suggested that if anyone had a grievance the right thing for anyone having a grievance to do was to go to the proper c-ourt. Consequently action was taken by a returned soldier, one John Graham, of Edmonton. On April 5, 1921, this man laid a criminal information before Lieutenant-Colonel G. B. McLeod, Police Magistrate for the city of Edmonton, charging a certain Edmonton millionaire with uttering a forged document in procuring a half-breed scrip. The result of the preliminary hearing before Magistrate McLeod was that Mr. Richard Secord of Edmonton, a prominent millionaire and the man referred to, was committed for trial before the first court of competent jurisdiction. That was in April 1921. The charge was that Mr. Secord had bribed a half-breed woman with $10 and a grey shawl to go with him to the Dominion Lands Office and there represent herself to be the holder of a particular certificate which belonged to a woman who was then living at Fort Rae. It was alleged that Mr. Secord had purchased the scrip from, I believe, Mrs. Elizabeth Hyslop, and had paid her a part of the agreed purchase price on condition that her expenses to Edmonton would be paid along with the balance of the agreed purchase price when the land was located. This scrip was located near Edmonton by the other woman, while Mrs. Hyslop was living about seven hundred miles northeast of Edmonton, near Lake Athabasca. As I have said, the result of the preliminary hearing was the committal of Mr. Secord for trial.
When we discussed this matter two years ago we spent a good deal of time dealing with the Secord preliminary trial. I want hon. members to bear in mind that this case was tried after the department had taken the stand that very little could be done by them, or that it was inadvisable for them to take any steps because it was almost impossible to get direct and reliable evidence in the matter. The complaint made by these half-breeds was not that any particular man, but that many unscrupulous speculators, had followed up the men who were issuing scrip to half-breeds, and had taken advantage of the ignorance 401
of these people. I want to read an extract from the Morning Leader, of Regina, in this connection. It refers to the trial at Edmonton and its result, and also makes reference to the amendment that was made in the Criminal Code. Most of the newspapers in the West during the year 1921 seemed to think that the amendment to the Criminal Code shut out the possibility of proceeding further with the Secord case. Be that as it may, here is the point:
That the objectionable amendment in question was designed to cover more than the Edmonton case appears to be more than likely, for more than one reputed millionaire in the West owes his financial position to the utilization of just such practices as those alleged in the Edmonton case. Saskatchewan is not without representation in this class of half-breed scrip millionaires whose shady practices had brought them within reach of the law until a kind-hearted government at Ottawa legislated specially for the purpose of relieving them of all further liability to prosecution for their criminal offences.
The foregoing is from the Morning Leader of Regina, Saskatchewan, of August 23rd, 1921. The point I make is that whether or not this amendment was retroactive and affected the Secord case, it did shut out the possibility of prosecuting others who might be guilty and against whom action had not been commenced at that time. Now, Mr. Speaker, let me examine the amendment itself. It reads:
Any offence relating to or arising out of the location of land which was paid for in whole or in part by scrip or was granted upon certificates issued to halfbreeds in connection with the extinguishment of Indian title.
This was inserted in the list of offences covered by the limitation of actions. In section 1140 of the Criminal Code we find:
That after the expiration of three years from the time of its commission no action shall be commenced if the offence be-
(1)	treason, except treason by killing His Majesty, or where the overt act alleged is an attempt to injure the person of His Majesty,
(2)	treasonable offences,
(3)	any offence relating to the fraudulent marketing of merchandise; or,-
Then this amendment was inserted as paragraph (4). At first glance, it would seem to deal merely with an ordinary fraud in connection with the location of land paid for in scrip. But apparently it covers any offence, no matter how serious it may be, if it is at all connected with the location of land which was paid for in whole or in part by scrip. If the guilty person keeps out of the way for three years, and action is not commenced, thereafter he is immune. I cannot see any reason for this limitation.
Half-breed Scrip

As I understand the
statute, action can be brought at any time within three years, and once information is laid and a warrant obtained the statute of limitations would not operate.

Forgery in connection with the title to other lands does not come within the statute of limitations, and the wrongdoer can be proceeded against even after the lapse of many years. And this is quite right. Such an offence is considered to be so serious, that the guilty person may be sentenced to life imprisonment. For subornation of perjury the punishment may be fourteen years' imprisonment. This restrictive amendment to the Criminal Code deals specifically with offences relating to the location of land paid for in whole or in part by scrip or granted upon certificates issued to half-breeds in connection with the extinguishment of Indian title; there is no similar limitation in respect to other cases of fraud of the same nature.
Will my hon. friend state what under the law is regarded as the commencement of an action?

I am not a lawyer, but I may say that in a case of forgery there is no limitation of three years, and I claim there should be none when the offence is connected with half-breed scrip. People throughout the western provinces to-day are convinced that this legislation, introduced within fifty-five days after Mr. Secord was com. mitted for trial in the city of Edmonton-the case having been started to demonstrate to the authorities at Ottawa that substantial evidence could be adduced in support of the claims of the half-breeds-some people I say are convinced that the amendment was passed to save, if not Mr. Secord, at least some others who possibly may have been as guilty as he in connection with the filing of other half-breed scrip in western Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope the House will accept this bill to restore the code as it was previous to 1921. As I say, the amendment created a very bad impression throughout the West and has tended to discredit our parliamentary institutions. Therefore I hope that parliament will repeal the objectionable amendment in order that any people who have a grievance may get redress through the courts, or possibly through an investigation by the government itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when a similar bill was introduced two years ago it was accepted unanimously by the House, and therefore I do

not see why I should object to this bill tonight. However, I do not think it is necessary as far as the special case is concerned to which my hon. friend (Mr. Kennedy) has referred. It was the opinion of the Department of Justice two years ago, and is still, that the amendment introduced in the Senate in the session of 1921 had no retroactive effect in that special case because the proceedings had been commenced before the amendment was enacted by parliament.

Would the
minister state what effect it would have in other cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure that in cases in which the limitation or prescription had previously applied, this law would revive the offence which had been prescribed under the amendment of 1921. However, as I said before, there is no objection on my part to the bill being accepted by the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I certainly do not rise to oppose the second reading, any more than I did two years ago. I had not the least objection to the bill passing then, nor have I now, and I db not complain at all of the hon. member's introducing a bill on this occasion. What I do complain of is the intimation that he still seeks to press, that the amendment of three years ago was passed for the purpose of relieving a wealthy man in Alberta, and his attributing to the government and parliament of that day this intention which, he says, has had so baneful an effect through his province. He tells us to-night-
Does the right hon. gentleman wish to deny that it has had that baneful effect?

Not at all, but the responsibility for that baneful effect is upon hon. friends to my left. That the baneful effect was there I do not dispute. This was part of the dust storm raised by hon. gentlemen to my left-I am afraid I must include also some in front of me-in that campaign. It was all part of a malevolent and wholly foundationless propaganda that the government was always the friend of the rich. In this particular case they said that the government passed through parliament legislation to relieve a millionaire in Edmonton, and did it after the Minister of the Interior, and the Prime Minister even, were warned of the great crimes that had been committed and after the Department of the Interior had acknowledged that they were

Half-breed Scrip
powerless and had sent those who complained of the crimes to the courts. The newspapers were full of it. As I explained two years ago, I never even heard about the amendment until I reached Alberta and found the press alive with this frightful allegation against the administration. I explained at the time that such a bill passed when a prosecution was on cou'ld have no effect on the prosecution. But of course that could not be accepted; it had to go forth for the political effect it might generate; it had to go forth that the government had used the instrument of parliament to save its friends of the wealthy class against the poor half-breeds who were seeking to prosecute. So it went forth and so the baneful effect was produced. When this repealing bill was first introduced in the House I urged that the original legislation never affected the Secord case at all. I explained it in the plainest possible terms-
What about the other cases?

Well, I am at the Secord case now. It never could have affected the Secord case, and it was the Secord case that was filling the province of Alberta.
I never heard of any other; in fact I never heard until now. If such a thing was mentioned two years ago it did not sink into my mind.
Did the right hon. gentleman read the petition that was presented to him?

I suppose I did. I do not doubt that there were general allegations in the petition, but if the hon. member ever attains office he will get a lot of petitions and he will not find it very easy to carry each line and each sentence in them for any great length of time in his memory. I am speaking of the Secord case. I made it clear it could not have applied; that no one with the faintest knowledge of law could have imagined that it would apply; that all it did was to place in the category of a three-year prescription this offence, the same as many others which were in a like category.
It would, of course, while it was in operation prevent prosecution of others where the offence dated back beyond the prescription fixed in the statute, but as to the Secord case it did not apply. I did not know anything about the amendment at the time, and as to those members of the House who were at that time members and are here to-night, I venture to say that not one of them recalls it even now. Very well; not only did I take
that position, but other hon. members of the party here took the same view, and the Minister of Justice was frank to state and state most openly and clearly that it did not apply to the Secord case; that such was his opinion and the opinion of his department. But the hon. member makes his motion to-night and does not inform the House of that fact; does not say, as I think he should have said, that it could not have been introduced with any reference to the Secord case at all. And I fancy he would hardly think there were some others who, we feared, might be prosecuted and whom we were going to shield. The motion to-night should have been divorced from all reference to any special case at all. If there is reason in the public interest that the amendment should pass and that the prescription should be removed, all right. The government accepts it; I personally have no objection whatever.
Just as a matter of information what reason was there for passing that soft of legislation in connection with scrip land more than in connection with any other forgeries?

There was no more
reason than for passing other legislation that many a time passes this House.
That does not explain it.
What about all the other prescriptive legislation in the statutes? Other forgeries were already prescribed.

That does not explain why
it was necessary in this particular case.

The minister who had
charge of the bill in the Senate-for the bill originated there-had the matter brought to his attention, I do not know by whom; I have asked him and he cannot remember by whom. But he mentioned to the Senate that he knew of one case in which he knew where prosecution had been entered alleging an offence some twenty years old. He knew of that himself, consequently he felt there should be a prescription, and this three years was inserted. That is all the connection he had with it. My hon. friend laughs.
That looks fishy.

It looks fishy does it?
Well the hon. member does not do credit to himself to reflect on the honour of another member of parliament unless he has some reason so to reflect.

I have the reason of the
circumstances that have already been explained: that special legislation was passed
Half-breed Scrip

at that particular time when a very shady transaction had taken place in connection with scrip lands. I have good ground for my suspicions.

Well the hon. member
can entertain the ground all he likes. All I am seeking to urge is this: That it could never have applied to the Secord case, could not have been dreamed by the member who introduced it to have applied. The member who introduced it is a lawyer of some standing; he could not have had any such belief. As to whether he had in mind someone else, I have his own word that he had not. I never heard of any other case myself. But if hon. members want this passed, why, it can be done. I notice that a point is raised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as to whether a repeal now would revive heretofore prescribed crime. I would not like to express an opinion on that myself, I never had the point raised; but I should have thought it would. Personally I earnestly hope that the actual state of the law is such that it will revive; that the legislation passes, and that the government of Alberta is free to go ahead full steam-and then we will see what will be the effects of this amendment..

Mr. Speaker, I think that when this amendment was brought in, the Attorney General of Alberta took the ground that it did apply to the Secord case. I realize that possibly he is not a competent authority to pit against the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen).
How could it apply if the information had been laid prior to the bringing in of that amendment?
I do not wish 'to discuss that matter. I am giving you the authority, and the opinion-
I would like to read the opinion of that man. If he said that, he is not fit to be attorney general.
I am very sorry that the hon. member makes a remark of that kind, for I understand that the present government is elevating him to the bench.
I doubt very much if he gave that opinion. I would like to see the opinion produced. I know who the gentleman was.

I hardly understand the leader of the opposition. Do I understand him to say that the attorney general did not make that statement?
{Mr. Forke.]

I can hardly believe that the Attorney General of Alberta gave the opinion that the legislation would apply to a case where prosecution was already entered, and if he did it would be a curiosity to have that opinion produced in this House.

I am sorry I could not produce the evidence other than what is contained in the press. I am quite convinced it was contained in the press of Alberta at the time. If that was not the ground he took, it seems to me a remarkable thing that the prosecution was dropped. I can hardly see what excuse he could give if he thought that it did not apply, for there had been a conviction in the lower courts. I think the leader of the opposition has possibly taken this thing too seriously in so far as it applies to the Secord case. I think those who would like to see this amendment go through have no ambition to prosecute that case in particular. I think they desire to clean up many of these cases, and there are many men in Alberta who profited largely in these matters. I think it would be a good thing to pass this amendment and let them take their chances. I am quite convinced that sufficient time has elapsed. No one will get an unfair deal of any kind; and those not guilty have nothing to fear. There is an element of suspicion in the whole transaction, as our leader (Mr. Forke) suggested a moment ago. At the time, it was thought possible that some prosecutions would take place, and I think members will agree , that there was a demand for that amendment from some source. Some felt that they had to take to cover, and they thought they needed that amendment. If it is the policy of the parliament of Canada to pi'ovide ways for people to evade their responsibilities, well and good; but on the other hand, if it is the policy of the parliament of Canada to see that criminals are brought to justice and have to take their chances under the statutes of Canada, then I think this amendment should be made.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
There seems to be an element of confusion in this matter, and perhaps if there was a little more law and a little less politics there would not be any difference of opinion among the members of this House. We are treated to newspaper extracts instead of to legal opinions, and so long as the law of the country is to be administered by the newspapers we shall probably have a very unique result, but one that, perhaps, will not always be in accord with law as a science.

Half-breed Scrip
There is no use in exchanging legal opinions in this House with gentlemen who profess they have no legal opinions, and who rely on the newspapers for their information as to law. The very extracts that have been quoted to-night show clearly that the newspapers have been actuated by political motives rather than by legal principles. We ought all in this House to be quite prepared to accept the legal opinions of the responsible officers of the Department of Justice. Two years ago when another gentleman, who had entirely the respect of this House was acting as Minister of Justice we had those principles enunciated by him. To-night, when a gentleman equally respected by the bar of Canada is occupying the position of Minister of Justice, we have those principles repeated without the slightest deviation, and we have not before this House one single syllable in support of the assertion that the Attorney General of Alberta ever took a position contrary to that enunciated by two Ministers of Justice of the present government.
There was a statement made by my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Stewart) that the deputy attorney general had apparently thought the prosecution could not succeed. That hon. member was not speaking at all in a legal sense, and two years ago I suggested, and I have never found that my suggestion has been met in any way that probably the difficulty in the Secord case was because they found they could not get the necessary evidence after a great lapse of time. That has sheltered many a criminal, great and small, in this country and in other countries, and there is no necessity to reflect upon the honourable gentlemen who occupy or have occupied distinguished positions in the province of Alberta. Every trial lawyer knows it is one thing to state an offence; it is another thing to prove-it. You can only prove it by documents or human instruments, and sometimes one and sometimes the other, and sometimes none, is available, and without strict proof we cannot and we ought not to obtain conviction. You should not obtain conviction upon newspaper articles nor upon political prejudice. If we come down to that the level of the country will fall very low indeed, and we shall not improve matters if we attempt to tinker with the criminal law here solely from a political point of view.
No one in this House, as I understand it, is objecting for one moment to the repeal of this legislation which is being objected to. At the same time there is no reason why
this House should assume that the Secord prosecution was one whit affected by that amendment which is so strenuously objected to. It was not, and it could not have been, and you can take what you like as the answer, but it must be one of a very few things. Either a blunder was committed by someone in knowledge of law, or the evidence was not available which would warrant the law officers of Alberta to assume that the prosecution could possibly be successful. I prefer the -latter alternative, having respect for the law officers of Alberta. But whichever alternative is correct, that matter was settled absolutely in Alberta by people who could not be considered as in any conspiracy or in any connivance with members of a former government of this country. They had it entirely in their own hands, and if Secord has escaped any punishment that he merited he escaped it by reason of some failure in the province of Alberta, and not by any action of this parliament.
Now we are invited to consider other criminals, or possible criminals, who have not been prosecuted. Every one of them could have been prosecuted. Within three years from the passing of that objectionable legislation no one laid an information. Why? The law did not stop it. Perhaps the facts were not available. I think we can go a little further than that. I look at the debates of this House of two years ago, and I find that the hon. gentleman who introduced the bill made extended reference, and I think he has repeated it to-night, to a certain petition which was said to have been presented to my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) asking, in effect, for an investigation of land frauds. He also presented quite fully to this House the reply of the Minister of the Interior, and while 1 do not wish to take up much time of the House, I think it is only fair to refer to a portion of the answer of the Minister of the Interior, who, as reported at page 3214 of Hansard of 1922, stated:
Since the beginning of 1900 about 4,800 claims have been satisfied by the issue of land scrip calling for some 1,153,092 acres nearly all of which have been located and patents therefor issued either to the grantees of the scrip themselves or to their assignees. Many of these patents covering thousands of acres were issued nearly 20 years ago, the titles passing through many hands, and to question such titles now would, in the opinion of the department, be very injudicious and could result in no benefit.
Moreover, many of the original grantees and witnesses are dead and it would be impossible, at this date, to locate many of the others or obtain satisfaction or reliable evidence relating to these transactions which took place so many years ago.
Half-breed Scrip

Now, if it is a matter of punishment, no one in this House wants to prevent the hand of justice falling heavily upon a man who has committed a crime. But time enough elapsed for anyone who knew the facts to enable a prosecution to be brought, and I presume successfully brought, against anyone who committed a fraud. The half-breed would not be particularly interested. They would get nothing out of the prosecution. Some one might be punished, but the halfbreeds would not be restored to their rights. The hon. gentleman who introduced this bill two years ago was pressing this matter, and I think I heard him read to-night this demand for an investigation. But will anyone show me how the passage of the bill that is proposed to-night will result in one iota of an investigation into these 4,800 cases in which there may have been, and probably has been, some fraud? When we find the whole strength of the case put upon the Criminal Code, coupled with the extracts from the newspapers, and coupled with the suggestions we have had, and I think the rather unfair suggestion from the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) I think I am not unfair in making the deduction that this assumes entirely a political aspect. If my hon. friend the leader of the Progressive party and his stalwart supporters want to help the unfortunate halfbreeds, why do they not introduce legislation into this House providing for that investigation, . accompanied by provisions which will restore to the half-breed the rights of which they have been defrauded? When they content themselves with animadversions upon the change of the law which they wish to get rid of, and do not follow up the desire for the investigation, then I stamp the attack as purely a political one, as malicious as it is insincere, and as dishonest in its character as the stories of the land frauds, as it seeks to destroy the character of a man who ought to be considered beyond the pale of such attacks.
Now, are we to have some measures which will restore to the half-breeds the rights which, it is said, have been taken away from them? What measure of compensation has been proposed? What honest endeavour has the gov-, emment been asked to make, and what honest assistance is the leader of the Progressive party prepared to give to restore to the halfbreeds anything which has been taken from them? Do they know of all the cases? Can they point to one case where such a thing has happened? They come here two years afterwards with no more and no less infor-
[Mr. Baxter !
mation than they had two j^ears ago. They come here with the eternal whine and eternal calumny and nothing better. No one objects to the passing of the bill, but what we do object to is the attempt to make the pas- ' sing of this bill a vehicle of political persecution.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext: I am not going to enter into any discussion of the merits of the case which my hon. friend may have had in his mind when he moved the resolution, but I do think that the Minister of Justice will be well advised if he does all in his power to pass this amendment. I have some serious doubts as to the form of the proposed) amendment, but that will be a matter for the committee to which the bill will be referred. I believe that there should1 not be in the minds of any of the people in Canada any idea that justice is being perverted in this country. I say I do not know whether it has been or not, but the hon. members on the other side who spoke on this subject must be aware of the fact that they had three years to lay the information in this case, and if they had laid an information they were not prevented-I am giving the opinion of a humble lawyer- ftom pursuing that criminal information to the end, by having a jury bring in a verdict either of guilty or of not guilty in the case of the parties who were charged, notwithstanding any legislation that might be brought down in this House.
You refer to the Secord case?

I am referring to any case this act might cover in any way. If there is an information, if the case is pending in court, unless there is something in the amendment which brings these informations to a conclusion immediately without going further, then the information may be followed, if the persons behind the information want to bring it to a conclusion, by having a jury return a verdict of guilty or not guilty. I do not know the facts of the Secord case, but I wish to say that if there is in the minds of hon. gentleman from the East, the West or the centre of Canada any idea that legislation has been instrumental in allowing criminals to get clear, then I say we should go into that matter and1 show the people who had that suspicion that the parliament of Canada will not be a party to that. That is the only reason I have risen. I think the Minister of Justice will be well advised if he does everything in his power to have the amendment

Halj-breed Scrip
to the Criminal Code passed; and then if my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) who, I believe is sincere in this matter, or his friends who are promoting the cause, wish to lay an information against Secord or others they will have an opportunity of doing so. May I point out that the limitations in the way of bringing criminal charges and in the way of actions at civil law are not new. We have various limitations; practically every criminal offence you can think of, outside of capital offences-I am not speaking by the book just now, but I mention those-has those limitations. There are limitations in civil matters, in the ease of slander, in the case of libel, and in the case of debt; and it may be the government of the day-I am making no charge against them has no thought in the world of letting Secord or anyone else go free, but I say again if there is a suspicion in the mind of any part of the general public in any part of this country that an injustice has- been done, or that^ an act has been committed whereby a criminal was prevented from being brought to justice, it should be remedied, and if the amendment of the hon. gentleman from West Edmonton is going to remedy that kind of thing, I would strongly advise the Minister of Justice to allow this measure to become law; and if criminals have escaped owing to the amendment, they may be brought to justice.

I know nothing about the facts of the Secord case, nor of any of the other cases, nor have I made any study whatever of the section in question; but as I sat and listened to the discussion in reference to the question of reviver, I was prompted to say just a word or two. It seems to me that the offence in question has not been extinguished at all. It is merely a case of limitation of prosecution being imposed. Let us assume for a moment that some one is charged with the offence in question after the passage of this proposed amendment, and counsel for the defence takes the point that the prosecution is not warranted owing to lapse of three years. I presume he would immediately be asked by the Crown prosecutor to cite his authority for his position. The limitation having been removed from the statute, it would not be there and could not be cited; there would be no section of the act stating that the prosecution must be commenced within three years. Therefore, I venture to suggest that if this proposed amendment becomes law, no matter how many cases there may be, the prosecution of them could be taken up and
proceeded with. There seems to be a consensus of opinion from all quartern of this House in favor of the amendment, by all means let it be passed, let the doors be opened wide, and if any persons have been guilty of any such offence as is suggested, they can be successfully prosecuted.

It seems
to me that it is a very absurd proposal at this late date to make retroactive legislation. As I understand this matter, although I have no knowlege of the Secord case, an information was laid and a limitation of action was passed concerning offences of that nature. The information having been laid in the Secord case and the amendment that has been passed not being made retroactive, it could not affect that ease. It was, therefore, open to the officers of the Crown or the informant or private prosecutor to press the matter from a preliminary trial to get the party accused committed for trial, then to have him brought before a grand jury, and if the grand jury found a true bill, to have him brought before a petit jury and either a verdict or an acquittal secured. As the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) and the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) have stated, statutes of limitation apply in all cases, both in civil and criminal matters. We have also other laws of somewhat the same nature, although they are not statutes of limitation, and those statutes have obtained for a great number of years. For instance, in some provinces there are statutes to the effect that a person cannot bring an action for the price of goods bought, if they be of a value of forty dollars and upwards, unless some memorandum appears in writing or some of the goods have been received and so on. This is commonly known as the statute of frauds.	These are restrictions on the
rights of people to bring actions. There are also limitations of actions for slander, actions for libel.	There are limitations in the
Criminal Code as to bringing prosecution in cases of assault, bribery, criminal libel. This is done for the protection of persons. Supposing such a limitation of action was not to be found in the statutes, insinuations might be made against a certain person; the action probably would not be brought for say ten or fifteen years afterwards, and the accused would be devoid of all his evidence that would enable him to make a complete and proper defence. The law in its wisdom has determined that it is absolutely essential to have limitations of action. Yet my hon. friend opposite seems to think that by this
Half-breed Scrip

amendment he is going to have this Secord case revived, I would say that would be an absolutely absurd thing to do. Secord, at the time the information was laid against him was undoubtedly in possession of all the evidence that would enable him to carry on his defence. The statute was passed. It probably was not passed to meet the Secord case; it was passed in order to protect the public generally. He probably has lost his evidence; he probably has lost his means of making a complete defence on the merits of the matter. Therefore, to come back to-day and say that Vte should pass an amendment to the Criminal Code enabling that particular case to be tried again is unfair. It would be just as well to say that, because we have discovered evidence to-day in regard to an assault that a man committed twenty years ago, we should pass an act stating that the limitation as regards action for assault should not apply to assaults committed twenty years ago.. We must have a termination in these matters. That was the wisdom of legislatures in days gone by; and so long as we tamper with these principles that have stood the test of time, we shall be legislating to meet mere insinuations as they arise. This is simply a statute of limitation of action, and I think my hon. friend should be satisfied with the law which is made, not for one case, but for all people.

We are gettting tied up in our discussion with the Secord case. I am not particularly interested in the Secord case; but I am particularly interested in this, that the contention of the department "no evidence was available" does not stand, and that this calls for an investigation. That result of the Secord trial demonstrates that the department was wrong, and I think that is sufficient for our purpose as regards this case.
As regards this cry about limitation of action, I am not a lawyer; I never studied law; but to-day I read in Crankshaw's Criminal Law this:
4n the common law there is no limited time for the prosecution of proceedings at the suit of the Crown; and therefore, the proceedings in all criminal cases, in relation to which the time is not limited by statute, may be prosecuted at any length of time after the commission of the offence.
That is where the time is not limited by statute.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Rights saved and continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will explain what he has in view in subsection 2.

I have had this matter
explained to me by a lawyer, and I understand, that, even if the amendment to the Criminal Code passed in 1921 were repealed now, should any irregularity be found to have occurred during any part of the time that the amendment has been on the statute books, that is to say from 1921 to 1924, the limitation would still apply and might be an obstacle in the way of complete justice in any case that might be brought up. This section was drafted by parliamentary counsel to meet that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is what I had in
mind when the motion was made for the second reading of the bill. There was some question as to whether, if the prescription had already operated, the offence could be revived by repealing the amendment. There occurred to me at the time the decision of the courts of England in a case practically similar to the matter under consideration. I understand that this is what the hon. member has in view by subsection 2. But this subsection is not drafted to meet the case, the subsection reads:
Any offences in violation of the provisions of the section repealed by subsection 1 of this section, and committed between the fourth day of June, nineteen hundred and twenty-one-
That is, the date of the amendment.
-and the date of the coming into force of this act-
The present act.
-shall be dealt with as if this act had not been passed.
If it is dealt with as if this act had not been passed this prescription would operate.

There is
evidently a mistake in the wording of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would suggest that
the hon. member move that we report progress, so that another draft might be made of the bill.

I do not know upon whom this drafting of the bill should reflect, or what it is intended to cover. It might be the subject of investigation in future parliaments. However, I should like to know what subsection 2 as drafted means when it refers to "any offences in violation of the provisions of the section repealed by subsection 1 of this section," and so forth. The section which it is sought to repeal is the section as to procedure, and that does not create any offence; it merely states that you shall not prosecute after three years. Some hon. gentlemen seem to think that this creates an offence. We have had views from hon. gentlemen who are not lawyers, and in the discussion of this matter I think that fact has been absolutely demonstrated.
Progress reported.
Mr. GEORGE BLACK (Yukon) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, respecting quartz mining in the Yukon Territory.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is rather
late, Mr. Speaker, and I would suggest, if the hon. member has no objection, that the consideration of this matter be deferred and that the House adjourn.

This bill has been up on
two occasions now and I am afraid that if it is not dealt with at an early stage of the session it is apt to go by the board. I do not think it can be called a contentious bill. It follows pretty much along the lines of orders in council which constitute the law at present regulating quartz mining in the Yukon territory. The chief object of the bill is to state in the form of an act of parliament the laws governing quartz mining in the Yukon, which laws are now embodied in a large num-
Yukon Quartz Mining

ber of orders in council. I am quite sure that hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that that is an undesirable method of government. Formerly the laws regulating goldmining in the Yukon were contained in orders in council. But because of the fact that the government was far removed from the scene of operations, veiy often the regulations were found to be very undesirable in their effect. In many instances the government was not well advised by its officers on the spot, and the advice given enured to the benefit of persons who had not the best interests of the country at heart; in other instances the advice showed a lack of understanding of what should have been done. Ultimately the Yukon was given a representative in parliament, and a bill governing placer gold mining was introduced and passed into law. That law has worked very satisfactorily.
Up to the present, quartz mining has been carried on under orders in council, but the time has at last arrived, as it did in respect of placer gold mining, when it should be regulated by an enactment of this parliament. In this bill I have followed the language of the orders in council for the most part, and it expresses the law as now in force. It contains no radical changes, and if it is passed no radical changes will be possible in future except by parliamentary sanction. To-day radical changes are made in the regulations without notice to the parties most concerned, and such changes are not always in the best interests of the industry affected. Changes are made at times which are found to be undesirable, and after a remarkably short period of operation it has been found necessary to make further changes. At the present time there is an order in council running in the Canada Gazette making most material changes in regulations which were issued as late as 1922, on the advice of officers of the government who are out of touch with the situation, but the government acted in good faith. These frequent changes would not be necessary if the law was enacted by parliament,. Each change has a disquieting effect on titles, property rights and methods of operation. I am sure that this is a necessary bill, and that if enacted it will be in the best interests of the territory and of the mining industry. If it is given a second reading, I propose to ask that it be referred to the committee on Mines and Minerals.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the second reading of the bill, provided that it goes to the committee on Mines and Minerals.

But I think my hon. friend will discover after the bill is in operation that quartz mining could be carried on much more acceptably by the old method of regulations. The complaint he makes that changes in the regulations prejudice the industry I cannot believe are well founded, because such changes apply not only to the oil industry but to other activities. If this bill is passed it will relieve the department to a considerable extent, because very frequently we receive requests for changes in the regulations. Each proposed change is carefully considered by the officers in charge, who have mining experience, and usually the changes are in the best interests of the industry. Once this bill becomes law, changes can only take place annually and upon the request of hon. members, perhaps at times when our officers have not an opportunity of making an investigation. However, the bill is quite acceptable to me provided it is referred to the committee on Mines and Minerals.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
